wlcrsj.text: A cyberattack on a U.S. government contractor has impacted the platform used by all federal bankruptcy courts across the country. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts published a statement on Thursday afternoon warning that a cyberattack on British multinational BAE Systems disrupted the Bankruptcy Noticing Center (BNC) — a system that produces and transmits bankruptcy notices for all federal bankruptcy courts. “The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts has been in communication with the impacted courts and is also coordinating with BAE Systems. BAE is actively investigating this incident and working to restore operations,” officials said. “As a result of the incident, all access to the BNC systems and websites that BAE operates on behalf of the judiciary and the related bankruptcy noticing process are unavailable at this time, including bnc.uscourts.gov, bankruptcynotices.uscourts.gov, notices.uscourts.gov, and the National Creditor Registration Service.” The incident has halted all production of bankruptcy notices as well. The office did not respond to requests for further details about the nature of the incident or whether data was stolen. BAE Systems is one of the largest defense contractors in the world and is deeply embedded in the U.S. Government — providing aerospace, weapons and information security services across several federal departments. A spokesperson for the company said they are “aware of a security incident that is isolated to the BNC system and have taken immediate steps to address it.” “We are coordinating closely with [the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts] on the response,” they added. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which typically handles cyberattacks on federal agencies, directed Recorded Future News to the U.S. Courts. The FBI did not respond to requests for comment. The attack on the bankruptcy court system comes weeks after Arizona’s state court system was breached and the information of more than 1.3 million people was leaked. Last year, U.S. federal court officials said they were working to bolster online security for sensitive documents and other case files in an attempt to block cyberattacks and data breaches. The move followed a major hack of the courts’ case filing system which officials feared exposed the identities of confidential informants in criminal cases. The federal courts docketing system was also attacked by hackers in early 2020. The U.S. government has been battered by cyberattacks in recent weeks, with incidents involving the Defense Department and the FBI. On Wednesday, the Department of Transportation confirmed that a safety agency contact center was temporarily taken offline after a contractor was hit with a cyberattack. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

mzuxz3.text: Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-110447, in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) for Nextcloud. Multiple administrator reports indicate that attacks began in mid-September, roughly a month before the formal security bulletin, the GitHub advisory, and CVE publication. CVE-2026-110447 impacts richdocumentscode versions before 26.4.303 and resides in the Nextcloud app’s mechanism for starting the bundled Collabora server. The flaw affects only the optional built-in CODE server app. Standalone Collabora Online servers, Docker and RPM/DEB installations, and Nextcloud All-in-One deployments remain unaffected, according to Collabora. The attacks involve sending a malicious request to the app’s proxy.php endpoint, triggering OS command injection. A key prerequisite for successful exploitation is that the built-in CODE server must be stopped (e.g., after a restart, upgrade, crash). Authentication or user interaction is not required. System administrators impacted by malicious activity reported attacks against multiple endpoints dating back to September 10. According to the reports, the attacker planted PHP webshells and used them to search for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets. Some users also reported that ransomware operators are exploiting the flaw, but BleepingComputer could not independently confirm this. System administrators are recommended to upgrade to version 26.4.303 or later, or remove the server app if not needed. The vendor warned that disabling the app is insufficient. Beyond the mid-September warnings from maintainers, a community warning was also published on October 3, urging administrators to update immediately due to ongoing exploitation. However, the lack of a CVE ID made it more difficult for administrators to pinpoint the issue correctly and implement efficient defenses. A study from cybersecurity company Second Security illustrates the gap between security fixes and formal vulnerability notifications. The firm analyzed real-world examples from open-source flaws and found that the median interval between public fixes and CVE publication was 39 days in August, up from 5.1 days in January. The researchers suggest that growing volumes of AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries are straining CVE processing and contributing to publication delays. Source: Second Security In many cases, the researchers found public exploit code emerged online within hours of a security fix and several days before the corresponding CVE was published. Second Security notes that the use of AI tools makes it easy for attackers to generate working exploits for published fixes. Examples of public exploits and CVE appearance timesSource: Second Security In Collabora’s case, the fix was committed on September 9, and version 26.4.303 was released on September 11. The advisory and CVE were published on October 14, a gap of more than four weeks. BleepingComputer contacted Nextcloud with questions about its response to the malicious activity reports, as well as details about the attacks and the number of impacted systems. Nextcloud told BleepingComputer that Collabora reported the vulnerability in mid-September and that an update became available through the app store. The company justified the disclosure delay by saying it gave users time to update and that it had not observed widespread exploitation. In a blog post earlier today about the activity, Collabora attributed the delayed announcement primarily to GitHub CVE-processing backlogs, which it said were under strain from increasing volumes of AI-driven security reports. 16st4el.text: A newly disclosed critical flaw in the Linux kernel allows code inside a virtual machine to read memory on the host computer it runs on. A researcher demonstrated the leak against Vercel's live cloud sandboxes, and Vercel confirmed it. The flaw, now tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and nicknamed PwnEscape, is in the Linux kernel's networking code, not in any one cloud's setup, so it reaches the shared layer that cloud providers use to keep customers' workloads apart. It was found in a Vercel security challenge and reported privately before any public release, and there is no sign it has been used in a real attack. What the Researcher Showed Paulos Yibelo of the security firm pwn.ai found that specially made network packets sent from inside a virtual machine could do three things, he explained in a technical write-up: read the host's memory, crash the host, and run code on it. All three come from the same kernel flaw. Vercel said in its report on the challenge that the memory leak was demonstrated against its production sandboxes. Each packet the guest sent out could carry back about 32 bytes of the host's memory, and the guest could keep going as long as it kept sending packets. The crash and code execution were observed only on the researcher's own machines, which were set up to match Vercel's. Two specially crafted packets were enough to crash a host and take down every sandbox running on it. Using the same flaw, the researcher then reached administrator control of a host, breaking out of the virtual machine. He stressed this was a lab result, "not a claim of root command execution in any vendor's production environment." "Our research ran through Omega-Pwn, an internal harness combining our own security research tooling with elements of SingularityNET's OmegaClaw architecture. It let us carry hypotheses, code traces, failed attempts, and experimental results across long-running research sessions. GPT-5.6 Sol was the primary reasoning engine. We directed the investigation, challenged its findings, and validated the interesting ones against actual kernel behavior on systems we controlled," Paulos Yibelo told The Hacker News. Vercel said no report in the challenge showed anyone reading a customer's files, secrets, or application data. How Severe It Is, and Who Can Set It Off The kernel's maintainers assigned the flaw CVE-2026-99999 and, in the published record, rated it 9.3 out of 10, or Critical. The U.S. National Vulnerability Database had received that entry but had not yet finished its own review. The same record lists the attack vector as local. In plain terms, the attacker has to already be running code inside a guest, as the researcher was. This is not a flaw that an outsider can exploit by sending packets across the open internet. It is not in CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities, and no real-world use has been reported. Why It Reaches Beyond Vercel Vercel Sandbox runs each customer's code in its own Firecracker microVM, a small virtual machine with its own copy of the Linux kernel, on bare-metal Amazon EC2 hosts. That microVM is the wall between one customer and the host, and between one customer and another. The flaw is not in that wall. It is in the Linux kernel's networking code, which the host runs. pwn.ai said Vercel's sandbox was already hardened beyond normal industry standards, with no misconfiguration it could find. Because almost every large cloud separates customer workloads on the same layer of the Linux kernel, Vercel said that a flaw there poses a risk to shared infrastructure rather than to any one provider. The Fix and the Fixed Versions The fix is a single Linux kernel change, commit 6785011f8b16, written by Red Hat's Michael S. Tsirkin and merged into the mainline kernel. It adds a check that a packet's checksum data cannot point into the IPv4 header before the kernel acts on it, and applies that check at five places in the networking code. The change is deliberately partial. Its author calls it "a defence in depth measure" and notes that a fuller check on the way packets enter the kernel still needs work. The maintainers backported the fix to the stable kernel branches. According to the CVE record, these are the first fixed versions in each supported branch: Stable branch First fixed version 5.10 5.10.272 5.15 5.15.223 6.1 6.1.190 6.6 6.6.159 6.12 6.12.113 6.18 6.18.57 7.2 7.2.11 Linux distributions ship their own kernels and often add this kind of fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's advisory and whether the fix is in the kernel the host is actually running, not only the number from uname. What to Do Update the host kernel to one of the fixed versions above, or to the vendor build that includes the fix, and reboot into it. Updating only a guest's kernel does not fix the host. The sources give no separate workaround for this flaw if you cannot update yet. Where patching has to wait, the usual step is to limit what a break-in could reach. Vercel said it keeps host kernels up to date, disables nested virtualization, and runs each microVM under Firecracker's jailer, which grants the microVM process only the permissions it needs. That does not fix the flaw, but it narrows what an attacker who used it could do. Found in a $1 Million Challenge The flaw was found in a two-week challenge Vercel ran in August that offered up to $1 million in total to anyone who could break out of its sandbox. No single payout reached that figure. The top reward per report was $50,000; Vercel paid $242,000 across 1,285 reports, and this flaw was the one Critical finding. pwn.ai said it found the flaw in three days using its own AI-assisted research system, with the model doing the source-code analysis and human researchers directing the work. The firm put the cost at under $700 in API tokens. It was the latest case of researchers using a large language model to help find and chain real flaws, after a separate team used one earlier this year to reach internal systems at OpenAI.

6zbabv.text: Google announced new AI-powered defenses against scam messages and call-forwarding abuse on Android, currently rolling out to eligible devices. The new measures aim to address the increased sophistication of scams targeting mobile users, including fraudulent bank alerts and voice-cloning attacks. “Mobile scams have evolved far beyond basic robocalls and phishing texts, turning into sophisticated operations that use spoofed numbers, fake bank alerts, and AI voice cloning,” Google says. “With scams growing harder to spot, it’s nearly impossible for users to catch every red flag themselves,” added the tech giant. Google says its existing Phone and Messages scam detection flags more than 5 million suspected scam calls and texts monthly, but the new measures are expected to catch even more threats. Cloud-based scam analysis The new protections focus on Google Messages and rely on cloud-based Gemini-backed analysis for complex conversations, scrutinizing them for signs of fraud. The system analyzes conversations with unknown senders within the encrypted Private AI Compute environment, protecting user privacy at all times. The new mode also adds on-device Gemini Nano (local AI model) checks for unfamiliar links using real-time web signals, plus clearer warnings before opening links from unsaved numbers. The new cloud-based protections are currently disabled by default, allowing users to activate them. Scam alert on MessagesSource: Google Other improvements Apart from the Google Messages protection, Google has also implemented the enhancements in other areas of the Android system: On-device scam detection in chat notifications, previously launched on Pixel, will reach hundreds of millions more users through Android device partners later this year. Android’s existing sensitive-information masking is now expanding to Chrome and Android WebView, hiding login fields and payment screens during live screen sharing. Android blocks apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warns users before manually entered MMI forwarding codes take effect. Call forwarding warningSource: Google Google is also expanding its verified bank calls system, introduced earlier this year, adding financial institutions from more. This system checks whether a real bank’s call center initiated an incoming call or if it is a spoofing attempt. If the verification fails, the call is automatically ended. Google says that since June it has blocked over 3 million fraudulent calls of this kind for Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. Revolut and other global financial institutions are also supported. Android users should upgrade to the latest release, keep apps updated, and independently verify caller/sender identities when receiving requests for account-related action or sensitive information. 16q9wuc.text: Powerful zero-click spyware is being delivered to individuals worldwide through targeted ads, new research shows — an alarming development in the spread of surveillance technology. Parallel investigations led by the digital forensic research institute the Citizen Lab and the ad tech-focused cybersecurity company Confiant documented how the Israel-based purported advertising firm Discover-Tech used digital ads to infect devices used by at least 45 journalists at Al Jazeera. The malicious infrastructure also served ads onto the internal networks of dozens of government agencies and international organizations, but the report did not say how many officials’ devices were compromised. Researchers found evidence that Discover-Tech ads were displayed on devices in “national-security-sensitive networks around the world,” including NATO, Citizen Lab said. Confiant separately analyzed targeting data and found evidence suggesting that the malicious ads were rendered on networks in the U.S. Department of Defense, Estonia’s Information System Authority (RIA), the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the International Criminal Court. Discover-Tech allegedly collaborated with the Israeli spyware company Candiru, whose product has long been used to snoop on members of civil society and was blacklisted by the U.S. Commerce Department in 2021. Candiru allegedly hired Discover-Tech to send the ads, the report said, and the mercenary spyware company used it to spy on Al Jazeera journalists and others. The ads “covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance,” the report said. The digital advertising firm, which Google and other major platforms have blocked in the wake of the research, has also worked with other Israeli spyware companies, allowing them access to ad platforms hosted by Google and Russia’s Yandex, Citizen Lab said. Discover-Tech allegedly served millions of ads that were used to monitor targets and break into their devices. Discover-Tech’s platform, known as Controlium, allows its spyware clients to “deanonymize, fingerprint and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them,” the report said. Deanonymization matches encrypted or pseudonymous data with public data, leading individuals to be unmasked. Candiru contracts with Discover-Tech to use its platform to deliver malicious ads, according to the report. Discover-Tech automatically executes malicious JavaScript code when an identified target visits a page with one of its ads. It avoids “directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads,” the researchers said. The Citizen Lab studied four billion Discover-Tech ad placement records and found that over just four months the corrupted ads were allegedly displayed on Android/iOS apps and nearly 200,000 unique websites. The Controlium software allows spyware firms to record calls, turn on microphones and siphon off messages and emails, the Citizen Lab said. In addition to government officials, Controlium has been used to infect devices belonging to reporters, dissidents, and embassy staffers. Discover-Tech serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem,” the Citizen Lab report said. “In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose.” By using Discover-Tech, spyware operators like Candiru could track and infect devices without facing traditional barriers like restrictions barring anyone other than government officials from buying the software and the need for using social engineering tactics. While there has been previous research suggesting that ad tech can potentially be used to facilitate spying, the new findings are far more definitive and detailed than what was previously known and represent the first time researchers have collected technical evidence backing up suspicions. Candiru and other spyware firms are not the only users of Discover-Tech, the report said. A different threat actor the researchers have named Dark Cartographer also uses the company’s software to take advantage of vulnerabilities in mobile carriers to tie device advertising IDs to phone numbers, a tactic the report said facilitated the mass-deanonymization of people online. The lack of regulation in the digital advertising ecosystem needs to change, the Citizen Lab said. “Ad vendors must significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers across the supply chain,” the report said. “They must rigorously and regularly vet, screen, and audit their business partners and hold them accountable for their own supply chains.” No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

j7vsws.text: Someone built a tool to steal data, then decided it should scare the victim for fun. Yes, that’s an actual feature. And somehow, it fits right in with this week's security stories.The rest gets interesting in different ways. A small permission can lead to a big theft. A trusted login can hide the wrong person. Old bugs are finding new victims, familiar tools are being put to strange uses, and some flaws are so simple you wonder how nobody spotted them sooner.There's a lot more hiding in the details, including a few twists you probably wouldn't expect. Here's what made the list this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. Active ransomware exploitation Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access. The vulnerability, disclosed in May 2026, has since come under active exploitation. "Because this access originates through an organization’s own VPN, malicious activity can resemble legitimate remote work and may go undetected until credential theft, lateral movement, data theft, or ransomware deployment is underway," ReliaQuest said. "Organizations should immediately upgrade affected deployments, disable authentication override cookies where they are not required, terminate all active GlobalProtect sessions after patching, and investigate unexpected connections, including sessions using hostnames such as 'kali.' Patching alone may not remove access established before remediation." Hybrid warfare escalates across Europe Russia is assessed to have escalated its use of hybrid, asymmetric warfare across Europe following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. "They do not involve troops moving across a country’s border or a state’s military dropping bombs on an adversary’s capital city," Recorded Future said. "Instead, they are a complex kit of psychological, cyber, and physical tactics meant to achieve several key aims: (1) Test the enemy’s defensive capabilities, as Russia evaluates whether to escalate aggression into a formal, kinetic conflict, (2) Degrade the enemy’s critical infrastructure, and (3) Sow an environment of fear in the enemy’s government and population to degrade the enemy’s ability to respond." DNS-powered wallet theft Infoblox has analyzed a cryptocurrency wallet-drainer kit, self-branded as Noir, that makes use of DNS TXT records to locate its hosted pool, which currently runs on Cloudflare Pages. It's delivered by means of a loader that queries the TXT record through public DoH services to learn which backend pool is active. "The drainer does not need a seed phrase, password, or private key," Infoblox said. "It tailors content to the user after receiving initial read permissions, developing a plan for the specific wallet. Then it obtains spending permissions that can look less alarming than a direct transfer and performs the theft from attacker-controlled infrastructure." It's suspected that the malware was created and maintained with AI assistance. Discord-based remote access threat A Rust-based remote access trojan dubbed CikaBika Bot has been observed being delivered via a document-themed lure containing a malicious LNK file and a PDF with an embedded payload. "The malware uses a Nim loader, PowerShell UAC bypass, and DLL search-order hijacking before leveraging Discord for C2, reconnaissance, remote execution, and data exfiltration through ngrok in observed malicious activity," Darktrace said. The malware also supports screenshot capture and file transfers. RAT combines theft and intimidation A Windows remote access trojan (RAT) called KGB RAT is being marketed on underground forums since late 2025 as being fully undetectable. It features a built-in crypter, HVNC, credential theft, ransomware, and an unusual set of psychological harassment capabilities, per Group-IB. "KGB RAT is, in practice, a full-featured malware package that gives attackers silent and persistent control over infected Windows machines," it said. "What sets it apart from comparable RAT families is not only its technical breadth — combining credential theft, keylogging, hidden desktop takeover, and ransomware in a single builder — but also a dedicated set of psychological harassment features, including screamer functions, jump scares, and forced blue screens of death. These 'fun settings,' as the developers themselves describe them, signal a threat actor profile comfortable weaponizing victim anxiety alongside data theft." A public disclosure referencing a KGB RAT server at version 0.1 dates to late January 2022, indicating the developer had been building and testing the malware for years before bringing it to market. Stealthy live-screen surveillance A multi-stage infection chain on Windows has been observed deriving a previously undocumented .NET RAT with live screen surveillance capability. It's been codenamed BotHelper RAT. "The first stage is a native x64 stager that fingerprints the host computer name, logged-on user, processor configuration, and installed memory, then connects to easyllms.xyz over HTTPS and retrieves a file named payload.bin from a path guarded by a long hexadecimal identifier, disabling TLS certificate validation beforehand," Point Wild said. "The second stage is BotHelper RAT. It copies itself to a hidden location, registers a scheduled task to relaunch every 30 minutes, patches the Antimalware Scan Interface, and registers with the same host that delivered it before polling a set of PHP endpoints for tasking." New Android anti-scam defenses Google said it's rolling out multi-layered protections across Google Messages and third-party messaging apps to protect Android users against mobile scams. This includes enhanced Scam Detection with Private AI Compute, link safety checks with Gemini Nano, and redesigned warnings before tapping unfamiliar links. Google also said it's bringing Scam Detection in chat notifications to warn users about suspicious messages directly from their notification shade to other Android devices in partnership with device makers. Other security improvements include automatic screen-share privacy to hide sensitive information in native apps, Chrome, and Android WebView, blocking apps from quietly enabling call forwarding in the background, and real-time verification for bank calls in collaboration with Banco do Brasil, Itaú Unibanco, and other leading banks. "Android checks incoming calls in real time to verify whether the bank actually initiated the call," Google said. "If an incoming caller claiming to represent a bank fails this verification check, Android hangs up the call and immediately alerts you." Since launching this feature in June 2026, Android has blocked more than 3 million spoofed calls from Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco alone. AI model theft defenses strengthened Anthropic has disclosed that new measures like preserved thinking, two-stage classifiers, and charging for requests that are blocked by our safeguards before Claude responds in its Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 models have reduced data harvesting through distillation attacks by about 90% to 99%. Enterprise browser security controls Mozilla has launched Firefox Enterprise, a browser iteration "built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements." Mozilla added, "IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience." Self-healing WordPress backdoor Wordfence has detailed an unusual malware that's installed as a must-use WordPress plugin and makes use of "several self-healing mechanisms in place in order to survive removal. It also makes use of EtherHiding, a technique that hides the location of the attacker's servers behind a smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain, making the command channel resilient to takedown." The malware is capable of establishing administrator access, hiding the rogue administrator account, harvesting administrator passwords, remote site modification, data exfiltration, and spreading to other WordPress installations on the file system. Stolen credentials expose GitHub data Meta said it's notifying about 1,500 people, most of them its own employees in the U.S., after unknown threat actors broke into some of the company's GitHub repositories. The intrusion, detected a few weeks ago, involved the use of an employee's stolen credentials. The access has since been shut down, according to SecurityWeek. XWorm expands surveillance capabilities The malware known as XWorm has transitioned from an infostealer to a full-blown surveillance platform. The malware's plugin count has expanded from 35 to 46. The latest versions detected since July 2025 are V6.4, V6.5 "XWorm Reborn," V7.2, and V7.4. "The Maps plugin provides victims' GPS location without triggering a user prompt," Netskope said. "The Microphone plugin streams live audio from the victim’s device. HBrowser gives operators interactive control of authenticated browser sessions without touching credentials, bypassing MFA entirely. Webcam capture is also available on demand." Higher rewards for memory-safety bugs Google has announced that it's raising bug bounty rewards for some Chrome vulnerabilities, with a focus on memory safety issues. While the company lowered standard payout amounts for some vulnerabilities in April, such as a base reward of $500 for memory safety issues, it has now quadrupled base rates for memory safety flaws to $2,000. Vulnerabilities in Chrome's browser, GPU, and network processes can now earn researchers up to $20,000. Post-quantum readiness warning Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, stating that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. "Organizations should begin now by inventorying certificate dependencies, assessing vendor roadmaps, identifying long-lived infrastructure, and creating non-production test environments," Microsoft said. "Early testing can surface compatibility and process gaps before post-quantum authentication is required at scale." AI tool credentials at risk A new malware-as-a-service (MaaS) infostealer written in Rust comes with its own loader and a built-in cryptocurrency clipper. "Warden Stealer is one of the first infostealers targeting configuration files and local data belonging to AI assistants and agentic coding tools," Gen Digital said. "Its builds are heavily obfuscated, morphed, and regularly updated to evade detection." Advanced browser data theft Newer versions of CastleStealer can "bypass app-bound encryption in Chromium-based browsers, execute commands remotely, and exfiltrate stolen information in small encrypted transmissions rather than a single large archive," according to Flashpoint. The C#-based stealer was first discovered in April 2026. AI developer credentials targeted The infostealer known as Aoki (aka Aokigahara) is targeting credential and session files used by AI coding assistants, including Claude, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor, Codeium, and Gemini. The stealer was first seen earlier this year. "API keys and Open Authorization (OAuth) or session tokens allow malicious activity to be carried out under a legitimate developer's identity and API quota," the Symantec Threat Hunter team said. "They can also expose connected repositories, cloud services and CI/CD pipelines linked to that account, and may bypass safeguards that assume requests originate from a trusted user." In a report published last month, Google-owned Wiz said AI service provider API keys are a hot commodity. "These AI credentials are highly lucrative; allowing attackers to freely run their own workloads or resell the access as part of the illicit LLM resale market," it said. "In addition, these keys can potentially grant access to historical chat logs that may contain sensitive corporate data, but we’re not aware of public occurrences of this scenario." Customizable MaaS infostealer K7 Labs has detailed a Python-based builder that is sold under a MaaS model and is used to embed an infostealer payload. "Rather than operating as a standalone stealer script, the builder follows a MaaS-style model," it said. "It allows operators to generate customized Windows executables using Nuitka or PyInstaller, with webhook configuration integrated into the build process." The stealer capabilities include anti-analysis techniques, persistence, credential harvesting, and data exfiltration. Cloud credential theft risk An SSRF vulnerability (GHSA-2phj-cp9f-qq6w, CVSS score: 8.5) in Harbor, the CNCF open-source container registry, can be abused by a registered user to steal cloud credentials. "Any registered user who can create a project can point a webhook at the cloud metadata endpoint and walk away with the server’s IAM credentials," OX Security said. Unauthenticated RCE chain A set of high-impact vulnerabilities in Adobe Experience Manager (AEM) can be abused to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). The chain combines four flaws: Unauthenticated DAM bulk import, stored cross-site scripting (XSS), unsafe XML parsing, and Groovy execution via /bin/asynccommand. The flaws affect only the cloud version of AEM and have been patched. Critical unauthenticated RCE Samsung has patched a critical security flaw (CVE-2026-110392, CVSS score: 9.8) in QA-Board that allows unauthenticated RCE. Samsung's QA-Board is an experiment-tracking tool that's used to organize, visualize, compare, and share research runs, specifically for algorithm and performance tuning. The problem stems from a case of improper neutralization of user-controlled data that could result in shell command injection. The vulnerability was flagged by Claude Opus 5.5. Linux root and container escape Security researcher Ziyi Guo has disclosed details of a critical Linux security vulnerability in NVIDIA's GPU Display Driver for Linux (CVE-2026-47595, CVSS score: 7.5, aka Bad UVM) that could allow an unprivileged user can write to read-only memory by taking advantage of the fact that the memory's permissions are not preserved. The vulnerability could be exploited to achieve code execution, escalation of privileges, denial-of-service, information disclosure, data tampering, and even a container escape. "By injecting our exploit code into nvidia-persistenced, we first force the hijacked process to execute a UVM-based local privilege escalation (LPE)," the researcher said. "Once the privilege barrier is crossed, we trigger the subsequent operations, ultimately granting us the ability to execute commands on the host with full root access." Active command injection attacks A command injection vulnerability in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) has come under active exploitation in the wild. The flaw affects customers using version 2.20 or later with statistics enabled, which is turned on by default. Successful exploitation could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on affected systems. It's currently not known how the flaw is being exploited, by whom, and who is being targeted. Critical unpatched SQL injection Rapid7 has disclosed details of a critical SQL Injection vulnerability in Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce (CVE-2026-108065, CVSS score: 9.8). "The exploit allows a malicious actor to read sensitive data from the database, or, if the database user has high privileges, run system commands on the database server," Rapid7 said. "The SQL Injection exploit can be leveraged to view sensitive information in the database, such as user PII and passwords. If logged in with DB admin privileges, the vulnerability can be exploited to run system commands on the server running the database." Four code execution flaws patched NSD has released patches for four security flaws (CVE-2026-101341, CVE-2026-101339, CVE-2026-101338, and CVE-2026-101337) that could be exploited to achieve execution of arbitrary commands. The vulnerabilities, credited to Qifan Zhang from Palo Alto Networks and Gaurang Maheta, have been patched in NSD 4.15.3 or newer. Potential VM-to-host escape The Xen project has published details of CVE-2026-79610, a race condition in Xen's grant-table mechanism that could be abused to compromise the security of a virtual machine host and allow an unprivileged guest to elevate its privileges to that of the host. All Xen versions from 4.0 onwards are vulnerable. The issue has been addressed in xsa517.patch. As mitigation, it's advised to use the "gnttab=max-ver:1" hypervisor command line option or the "max_grant_version=1" guest configuration option for guests. The project maintainers credited Anthropic's Claude Opus with the discovery and Teddy Astie of Vates for diagnosing it as a security issue. SYSTEM-level remote code execution A Windows security vulnerability in MyReport Updater 2.1.1 can permit an attacker to seize control of a machine, including remotely, without authentication. "An attacker with standard user privileges can set an arbitrary reference server," Quarkslab said. "If MyReportUpdaterService can contact this server over gRPC on TCP port 9095, the attacker can write files into a chosen directory with NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges. The attacker can use this file-write access to place a DLL that will be loaded by a privileged process. The DLL code is then executed with high privileges. This vulnerability gives full control of the Citrix server. It can also affect other machines where the vulnerable MyReport solution is installed." If there's one thing this week's stories make clear, it's that attackers don't always need a clever trick. Sometimes a stolen login, a forgotten setting, or one small mistake is enough. And even when the bug gets fixed, the trouble it caused might still be sitting there.The lesson is pretty simple: don't just check what's broken. Check who got in, what they touched, and whether they can come back. Keep an eye on the things everyone assumes are safe. Those are often the ones nobody looks at until something goes wrong. That's it for this edition. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

gkosnb.text: A proxyjacking campaign has impacted devices in 34 countries, monetizing victims’ internet connections through a commercial residential proxy network. The operator installed Pawns.app, a legitimate bandwidth-sharing application that lets users earn money by sharing their internet connections, on devices without the owners’ consent. Pawns.app account holders are rewarded for allowing traffic from other users to flow through their network, provided it runs on trusted, non-blocking IP addresses. By installing the app on multiple systems, the attacker likely accumulated larger payouts. Source: GreyNoise Threat intelligence company GreyNoise discovered the campaign while investigating suspicious activity at an unnamed organization, and identified at least 143 compromised devices worldwide. According to the researchers, the attacker leveraged several vulnerabilities to breach edge devices and install the Pawns.app software: CVE-2024-3272 and CVE-2024-3273 in D-Link ShareCenter NAS CVE-2021-44228 in Ubiquiti UniFi Video NVR CVE-2025-31324 in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer The researchers also observed targeting of Hikvision and Dahua DVR/NVR devices, but did not specify the vulnerabilities exploited in these systems. GreyNoise says that, in some cases, the attackers configured SSH key authentication as a backup access method. Configuring SSH accessSource: GreyNoise Even legitimate proxy networks can route suspicious traffic through volunteer-operated nodes due to insufficient oversight, potentially resulting in IP address blocks for participating users or exposing them to allegations of involvement in illegal activities. The FBI previously warned about such networks being used to carry out large-scale credential stuffing attacks against online platforms. GreyNoise provides a free service (account required) for users to check if their IP address is part of a known legitimate or “gray” proxying service. It is generally advisable to avoid downloading software from untrusted sources, as purportedly free software may contain malware that enrolls devices in residential proxy networks. Threat actors also commonly exploit known vulnerabilities in internet-connected devices. Keeping NAS devices, video recorders, and other internet-facing systems updated can significantly reduce the risk of compromise. However, users should also use strong credentials, a secure configuration, and restrict network access. 10ek25h.text: A threat actor uploaded malicious packages to the Arch User Repository (AUR) that impersonated two popular helper tools, yay and paru. AUR is a community-maintained, widely-used package index for Arch Linux and derivative distributions that hosts package build scripts (PKGBUILDs) for third-party and proprietary tools, beta, or older package versions that are no longer available via the official Linux distribution channels. The repository has recently become a target of malicious campaigns, including an attack in June in which 400 packages distributed credential-stealing malware with rootkit capabilities. Another campaign in July prompted Arch to temporarily disable package adoption. The latest campaign was detected on October 13 and involved malicious packages uploaded by a user named “marchos1as” under typosquatted names mimicking the yay and paru command-line tools. Also known as AUR helpers, these tools simplify software management on Arch Linux by streamlining the retrieval and installation of user-contributed packages. A thread on the Arch Linux mailing list named "hundreds of aur packages were mass uploaded with malware" alerted users of the malicious uploads. In minutes, community members confirmed that the packages contained legitimate upstream code combined with a malicious installation script that executed a remote shell script with root privileges. “The package presents itself as a straightforward repackaging of the legitimate 'yay' AUR helper (same upstream URL, same source tarball), but the package name 'yyay' and the malicious install scriptlet reveal it is a trojanised impersonation designed to blend in with the real package,” AUR maintainer Andreas Reichel warned. Another maintainer, Emiliano Gandini Outeda, listed some malicious packages that triggered an alert on his system using rules in his open-source application security tool, TrustSight. The AUR team banned the account belonging to marchos1as and removed the malicious packages from the repository. Reichel says that the payload delivered this way was fetched through a Wayback Machine URL that pointed to a personal repository (hellscripter/install-scripts) hosted on the Russian hosting service GitFlic. Potential links to npm worm A recent report from application security company SafeDep documented an npm campaign dubbed "DirtyBlanket" that fetched code from a ‘hellscripter/install-scripts’ repository on Codeberg. The researchers found a Linux worm that deployed the CHAOS remote-access trojan disguised as a font service, which also injected a loader into AUR packages. Furthermore, an OSV advisory on the "DirtyBlanket" activity describes the same Wayback Machine and GitFlic domain. Despite the connections, there is currently no confirmation that the two operations are related. Arch users who downloaded the suspicious packages should assume that their systems were compromised and take immediate remediation action.
