1jd6law.text: Candiru, an Israeli maker of spyware sold to governments, infected devices at the news network Al Jazeera through ordinary online ads, in attacks that needed no click or other action from the user, researchers at the Citizen Lab said Thursday. The hidden attack code ran the moment an ad loaded on the screen, and in some cases the ad loaded out of sight, in the background. The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, said this is the first public, technical confirmation that mercenary spyware, meaning hacking tools sold to governments, has reached real devices through targeted ads. The method had been described before from leaked company documents, but not shown in a live attack. The researchers recovered the spyware itself from one device, but not the exploit that breaks into the browser or app to install it. That first break-in step is described from how the attack was set up, not from captured code. How the Attack Worked The ads were placed by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a normal digital advertising firm. Each ad carried a small piece of code that, when the ad loaded, quietly sent the device's advertising ID and internet address back to a Discover-Tech server, the researchers found. That server decided whether the device belonged to a target. If it did, the server sent back attack code for the browser or app to run. If it did not, the server sent nothing. Because the ad itself carried no attack code, the ad networks that delivered it had nothing harmful to detect. At Al Jazeera, at least 45 devices were targeted in 2024 and 2025, the Citizen Lab said, and it linked the attacks to Candiru with high confidence. The researchers did not say which government was behind the operation. The network gave the researchers its traffic logs. On infected devices, the logs showed the same order each time: first contact with a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru server that screens the device, then a command-and-control server that runs the spyware. Al Jazeera also pulled one Windows program file off a compromised device. Its code used the same distinctive techniques as a Candiru tool the Citizen Lab took apart in 2021, which is the basis for the high-confidence link. Al Jazeera staff were targeted once before. In 2020, dozens of its journalists' iPhones were hacked with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware, in a different operation that used a different method. Who Discover-Tech and Candiru Are Google and the advertising trade group IAB Europe had both listed Discover-Tech as an approved ad vendor from 2020 until this month. The company was registered in Israel in 2020 and is led by its chief executive, Dekel Boni. Candiru is one of the better-known names in the spyware trade. The United States put it on a trade blacklist in 2021 over spyware used to target government officials, journalists, and activists. In 2025, its assets were bought by a U.S. investment firm, Integrity Partners, and moved into a new company, reported to be Integrity Labs, that the sanctions do not cover. What the Platforms Did After the researchers shared their findings, Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their vendor lists in early October, the Citizen Lab said. Google cut off the company's access to its ad exchanges, Beeswax removed it, Vungle paused its access for a review, and Eskimi blocked its accounts. Google told Reuters it had worked with the researchers and removed Discover-Tech "for systematically violating our policies." IAB Europe said it suspended the company after an audit found policy violations. Comcast, which owns Beeswax, said it acted "following recent activity." Discover-Tech, Candiru's owners, Al Jazeera, and the Russian ad network Yandex did not respond to Reuters. Discover-Tech's website was still online on Thursday and said nothing about the findings. How Far the Ads Reached Discover-Tech's reach went far beyond Al Jazeera. On one of its platforms, the company placed nearly four billion ad bids between March and June 2026, the Citizen Lab said, and the ads carrying the hidden callback code appeared in about 75,000 phone apps and 120,000 websites. Confiant, a U.S. ad-security firm that investigated alongside the Citizen Lab, put Discover-Tech's traffic at roughly 10 million ads a day. The ads turned up on the networks of governments and large institutions, the Citizen Lab said, including NATO, the United Nations, European Union bodies, government offices in about two dozen countries, chipmakers, and news organizations. An ad appearing on a network is not proof that anyone there was infected. It shows only how widely the system could reach. Confiant found that the small number of ads it could tie directly to Candiru were low-volume and mostly reached home and mobile internet connections, rather than the sensitive networks themselves. What Defenders Can Check Both groups published the web addresses and files associated with the operation, so defenders can block them and search their own records. Organizations whose staff may have seen the ads, especially on the networks named in the report, can look for the attack's order of connections: a device reaching a Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru screening server, then a command-and-control server. Among the published indicators: SHA-256 (recovered spyware sample): 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8 Domain (Discover-Tech ad server): mtrtb[.]com Full list: the indicators in Confiant's report, including the command-and-control servers. Security researchers have warned for years that the ad-buying system could be turned to this use. In December, leaked documents tied the spyware maker Intellexa to a similar ad-based tool called Aladdin, though no live infection through it had been shown.

1sk9stz.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Cyber Espionage / Malware The threat actor known as Silent Lynx has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The activity, observed from June 2025 through August 2026, involves four different infection chains that make use of macro-enabled documents, PS2EXE downloaders, GitHub-hosted PowerShell, and crafted WinRAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088. The attacks lead to the deployment of custom reverse shells like FoalShell, Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell that facilitate interactive remote access to compromised hosts, according to Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group, which are tracking the campaign under the monikers UAT-6275 and TAG-193. "UAT-6275's targeting is concentrated in Central Asia, and the wider CIS region," security researcher Ashley Shen said. "Across the reviewed campaigns, observed victims and lure themes span nine countries: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Belarus." Silent Lynx was first publicly documented by Seqrite Labs in early 2025, highlighting the threat actor's attacks on embassies, lawyers, government-backed banks, and think tanks across Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan. It's assessed to be a Kazakhstan-nexus threat actor active since at least 2020, sharing overlaps with other clusters codenamed YoroTrooper (aka Comrade Saiga, ShadowSilk, and SturgeonPhisher), ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Tomiris. It's suspected that both UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper are part of the same broader activity cluster, although no direct indicator or toolset overlap has been observed between the two. Earlier this year, VMRay disclosed that a threat cluster it tracks as Hydra Saiga compromised at least 34 organizations across 8 countries since December 2024, with reconnaissance efforts extending to over 200 additional targets across the world. It's worth noting that both Comrade Saiga and Hydra Saiga refer to the same threat actor. The "hydra" prefix in the tracking alias is a reference to the adversary's heavy focus on breaching infrastructure linked specifically to water resources in Central Asia using a mix of custom implants written in Rust, Go, and Python and Living-off-the-Land techniques. Attack chains mounted by the threat actor involve the use of spear-phishing emails containing diplomatic relations, international trade, energy, and aviation-themed decoy documents. No less than eight campaigns have been identified across the region between January 2025 and May 2026. The phishing emails are sent from compromised government accounts and make use of official-looking documents to lend the social engineering attack a veneer of credibility. "Identified lures included a diplomatic letter addressed to Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal concerning Russia’s Orsk Oil Refinery," Recorded Future said. What's more, three publicly accessible staging directories linked to the threat actor have been found to host Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2025-25257, an SQL injection flaw in Fortinet FortiWeb, suggesting a possible expansion of the threat actor's operational capabilities. Infection sequences have been found to employ four different pathways - June 2025 - Using macro-enabled Word documents to download and run a second-stage binary. July 2025 - Using downloaders built with PS2EXE, a tool that packages PowerShell scripts as Windows executables, to fetch reverse-shell payloads and create scheduled tasks for persistence. October 2025 - Using a malicious shortcut (LNK) within a RAR archive to launch PowerShell responsible for retrieving and executing a GitHub-hosted script that provides remote shell access. Subsequent iterations also download PickleShell and stage it in the Windows Startup folder so that it's automatically launched every time a user logs in to the system. April 2026 - Using a RAR archive that exploits a WinRAR flaw (CVE-2025-8088) to drop PickleShell in the Windows Startup folder. The April 2026 infection chain marks the first time UAT-6275 has weaponized a security flaw as part of its malware delivery methods. "UAT-6275's sustained activity and adoption of new delivery techniques suggest the group will continue pursuing access to government organizations across Central Asia and the CIS," Talos said. "Its interest in environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure reflects the intelligence value of regional diplomacy and resource management."

18gist7.text: A cyberattack on Britain’s Legal Aid Agency (LAA) stole far older and broader records than the government previously disclosed, officials said Wednesday. While initially claimed to have affected people who had used the service since 2010, the breach is now believed to include about 250,000 records predating 2007 and to include data on additional people who were being supervised by the probation service. Justice Minister Sarah Sackman described the incident as “significant and complex” in a written statement to Parliament. She explained the cyberattack “happened because criminals were able to exploit vulnerabilities in the LAA’s IT systems and gain access to systems containing personal information. They then copied and exfiltrated some data held by the department.” The agency disclosed last May that hackers accessed data from people who applied for legal aid through its online service since 2010, potentially compromising data including criminal histories. At the time, charities warned the data — believed to have been stolen by cyber extortionists — could contain sensitive information about women and girls who survived domestic abuse situations. In an update published Wednesday, the Legal Aid Agency said continuing forensic analysis found more data was accessed than initially believed. “The vast majority of the LAA data relates to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and May 16, 2025, or to cases that were live during this period,” it said. “However, we have now confirmed that approximately 250,000 records predate 2007. The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978.” According to the forensic analysis, the stolen material also includes probation data covering names, dates of birth, nationalities and case reference numbers. “It is important to put this updated information in context,” said the agency. “The presence of records predating 2007 does not mean that everyone who received or applied for legal aid, or otherwise interacted with the justice system before 2007, has been affected.” It said the information exfiltrated varies between individual cases but can include full names, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, ZIP codes, equality monitoring codes, case start and end dates, costs claimed, the amount of VAT claimed or paid as well as codes indicating the type of legal aid received. Other categories include financial assessments of defendants and their partners, details of bank accounts and property, and in some cases partially redacted payment card details. The names of judges, defense and prosecution lawyers, and court reporters involved in Crown Court trials over the same periods were also taken. So were details of opposing parties in some civil cases, according to the update. The agency said the breach was hard to assess because much of the stolen data was “unstructured, fragmented, or incomplete.” It added that earlier public statements reflected the best information available at the time. Sackman told the House of Commons that the department has no indication the stolen data has been published or shared — a shift in view from May 2025, when a ministry spokesperson told Recorded Future News that its publication was a question of “when, not if.” The hackers had claimed to hold data on more than 2 million people and threatened to release it unless they received payment. The British government has a longstanding policy of refusing to pay extortion demands. Sackman said the ministry has since strengthened authentication and access controls, improved security monitoring and begun retiring or isolating higher-risk legacy systems. It continues to work with the National Crime Agency, the National Cyber Security Centre and the Information Commissioner's Office, the U.K.’s data protection regulator. No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

yrpqjw.text: A long-running Traffic Distribution System (TDS) known as Help TDS to a Russian-language affiliate program called Hotejka, which appears to be a rebrand of a traffic monetization operation dubbed ROI777. Help TDS is assessed to be active since at least 2017, offering PHP code templates to partners and affiliates that are installed into compromised websites with an aim to direct unsuspecting users to tech support scams. These scams make use of full-screen browser manipulation and exit prevention techniques to serve bogus Microsoft Windows security alert screens instructing victims to contact a Windows Support number to address the problem. "Help TDS delivers tech support scams (TSSs) that direct users to call centers, where social engineering is used to convince them to install remote desktop tools," Infoblox said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It's not simple credit card fraud: it's remote access, living-off-the-land malware operations. Once in, the threat actor can exploit the victim time and again." Help TDS's evolution was documented by GoDaddy in August 2025, highlighting the threat actor's use of a malicious WordPress plugin named "woocommerce_inputs" on thousands of websites to steal WordPress user credentials and facilitate the malicious redirections by fetching the URLs from its command-and-control (C2) servers. The plugin, or alternatively a custom HTML block, is injected into the sites by Hotejka's affiliates. Historical tracking of malicious redirect chains has also uncovered that Help TDS has routinely handed off traffic directly to VexTrio Viper, a cybercrime operator that runs an affiliate program to enable scams, riskware, spyware, adware, and pornographic content. The latest findings connect the TDS to Hotejka, which, in turn, is suspected to be a successor to ROI777, an entity that was exposed by Guardicore Labs (now part of Akamai) in June 2018 in connection with a traffic manipulation and cryptocurrency mining campaign codenamed Operation Prowli. The activity involved the compromise of vulnerable servers to deploy a malware named r2r2 and then leverage them to mine cryptocurrency. In tandem, WordPress sites and servers running other content management systems (CMS) were exploited for traffic monetization fraud. "Traffic monetizers, such as ROI777, buy traffic from 'website operators' such as the Prowli attackers and redirect it to domains on demand," Guardicore Labs noted at the time. "Website 'operators' earn money per traffic sent through roi777. The destination domains frequently host different scams, such as fake services, malicious browser extensions and more." The rebrand is believed to be driven by the leak of data obtained from ROI777's servers in March 2018, around when it was operating Disposable TDS, a precursor to Help TDS. The published details included Telegram identities of its users and details of multiple campaigns. The connection between Hotejka and ROI77 doesn't end there, for GoDaddy also found that "roi777[.]com" was one of the historical C2 domains used between 2018 and 2020 to fetch the redirect domains. "[Hotejka's] affiliates range from spam operators to website compromisers," Infoblox said. "Potential victims are redirected into the TDS from these affiliates via special URLs provided by Hotejka. The TDS then evaluates the user via browser fingerprinting and location to determine the course of action." A TDS functions akin to a relay, intercepting internet traffic from compromised websites, malicious ads, social media posts, or SEO spam, analyzing the visitor, filter traffic based on predefined criteria (e.g., geographic location, device metadata, IP reputation, and headless browsers), and dynamically route them to scams, browser lockers, or malware drops. "Help TDS and its precursors are the routing decision infrastructure for a small affiliate program," Infoblox explained. "Other threat actors, for example ones who have compromised websites, send potential victim traffic to the TDS through specially crafted URLs." The TDS is believed to be implemented on Keitaro, an advertising performance tracking platform that's known to be abused by various threat actors. Some of the initial Help TDS lures prompt users of an impending Windows update, followed by a warning that the machine has been disabled by Microsoft, tells them not to restart the computer, and that a "computer lock" has been put in place to block illegal activity. The scareware prompt is designed to persuade the victim to contact the Microsoft Technical Support team. Should the victim make the phone call, the threat actor on the other end instructs them to download and install a free remote desktop tool like Ultraviewer to gain complete control of the infected machine. The fingerprinting step determines whether to route the user to either the tech support scam or to another affiliate marketing platform, which then evaluates the device again and resells the traffic. These pathways lead to scam landing pages with fake CAPTCHA checks to enroll the victim's browser to push-notification spam. "Historical DNS records, loyal use of other affiliate advertising platforms over the years, and consistent command-and-control (C2) mechanisms give us a high degree of confidence that ROI777 and Hotejka are one and the same," Infoblox said. Messages posted by Hotejka on their Telegram channel (@hotejka_hot) demonstrate their criminal intent by advertising forced browser extension installations and tech support landing pages that are "very difficult to exit." In one post dated July 17, 2026, the operator claimed a "small call center in Germany will handle 50-100 calls per day." Since April 2026, the scams are run on free Cloudflare Pages sites (*.pages[.]dev), with the threat actor creating roughly 300 disposable pages per day. Over 20,000 such domains have been detected since then. In recent years, Hotejka has also been observed using different aliases on forums like CrackingX, seeking traffic from email spam and access to WordPress admin panels for prices starting at $100. In all, about 20 different affiliates, including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay, send traffic to Help TDS. These operations are known to heavily target WordPress sites to redirect victims to scams and malware. "Hotejka/ROI777 has been loyal to the two affiliate platforms since 2017, and we believe that loyalty has paid handsomely," Infoblox said. "Using DNS volumes observed over the past 8 years, our ability to use affiliate IDs to track traffic over time, and commonly cited payout figures for affiliate advertising in general, we suspect that the two European programs have paid them at least a few million dollars (USD)."

1xcsnze.text: With the rise of AI pentesting, a lot of people are wondering if it’s as good as a human. Having started as a pentester twelve years ago, and having moved through similar roles to working on Intruder’s AI pentester, I've come to understand the advantages and disadvantages of both. Here’s how they compare. The strict methodology was never the good bit You may expect AI pentesters to follow strict methodologies in the way that many human pentests do. At Intruder, we experimented with this approach early on - structured systems where each agent had a specific vulnerability type to look for. What we found was that agents would miss things outside their remit entirely, or miscategorize what they did find as the one thing they'd been told to look for, causing confusing reports. A complete lack of structure also failed to produce good results, as completely free agents without any guidance couldn’t break down and manage large applications properly. They could find interesting things, but at the cost of missing a load of other vulnerabilities in our targets. We’ve put a lot of testing into finding the balance between these approaches, and settled on giving agents freedom with broadly defined roles to help them approach and manage large applications, and stricter guardrails to stop them causing damage. This does mean that our AI pentester doesn’t tick off the parts of a methodology document that you’d typically see in a human pentest. That may make some people uncomfortable - a strict methodology gives people assurance that someone has gone through your application and tested everything on the list. An unauthenticated SQL injection needs to be found, and a checklist is there to make sure it does. The methodology gives a lot of people the idea that a human pentest is a perfectly repeatable product, as any tester will be able to follow the methodology, and everything important will get found. The reality is a lot more nuanced than that though, as pentesting is a skilled job, and many of the most impactful findings on a pentest will come from the tester being experienced in noticing weird behaviours and following up on them. For our AI pentester, we ended up with much more interesting and impactful results by not trying to guide our agents through specific vulnerability types. A good example is a complex authentication bypass the agents found that had been sitting in a codebase through five years of pentests without any human testers picking it up. The mechanics of that issue mean that you’d never think to write a testing guide that could be strictly followed to identify it, and if we’d tried to limit our AI pentester too much it never would have found it either. You could say that only finding the common things would still be pretty good, but there's such an array of vulnerabilities that aren't common that you find during a pentest. And just because they’re not common, it doesn’t mean that an attacker can’t find them too, especially now AI is being used to enable attacks more. A strict methodology being carried out by a competent tester only ever provided a low baseline of reliability, and it didn’t even do that perfectly. What makes a pentest good is the part that a skilled tester does outside the checklist, and that's where AI thrives - following its nose through your application and finding the things that were never going to make a list. What they know, and what they can’t ask Our AI pentests take a white box approach, which means the agents get the source code. They work through the entire codebase and build a picture of not just what every page is, but how the application is meant to function and what requests can be made. Doing this to the level of detail that the AI is able to isn’t feasible for a human pentester during a typical time window for a pentest. The AI pentester also builds up a sense of what the application is for, and a good example of this is access control - it doesn’t need to be told that low privileged users shouldn’t be able to reach admin functionality, or that a particular bit of data is sensitive. You can give them extra information as well, just like a human tester. For example, people often specify that they’re worried about their customers being able to access each others’ data, and the pentester has done a great job of focusing on these issues and identifying a lot of them. What the agents can't do is ask you for anything you didn't already give or tell them. If I don't understand what a part of an application does while I’m doing a pentest, I can ask my contact, and those conversations can be very useful for testing the application properly, and assessing risk in the final report. I can also clarify the scope with my contact if needed, or ask for permission to verify something when I’m unsure if there’s a risk of disruption. We’ve had to deliberately make our AI pentesting agents cautious on this front to avoid going out of scope. Neither finds everything The freedom that lets AI pentesting agents find something like a complex auth bypass is the same thing that makes them less predictable. They decide where to dig, and that won't be identical every time. But pentest results have always varied with the person doing them. It's why many consultancies will rotate your tester each year - different people find different things on the same application. This comes down to people’s experience, specialisms, and incidental knowledge. I’ve found issues because of a blog post or specification I happened to read years earlier and was left sitting in the back of my head. And even the things on a checklist get missed sometimes. People are fallible, and covering an entire application methodically over multiple days can be hard. Consistent coverage is something we're actively working to improve, but it’s not something that was ever offered perfectly from anyone. It's why every human pentest report comes with a disclaimer saying as much, even though most people read it as a formality. The remediation I couldn’t have written Every pentester has strong opinions about what makes a good report. I’ve built up many of my own over the years, as have the rest of the current and former pentesters at Intruder. These opinions are what we built our report around. The executive summary is the hardest page of a report to get right. For a lot of people it's their entire experience of your work, and at a good consultancy a lot of effort goes into it. We’ve worked to get to the point where the agents are now writing genuinely good ones, and I often read them first on our own reports to get a good overview before diving into detail. Where they're still off is scoring risk. They rate things higher than I would, partly because they can't have the conversations with you that would bring a rating down, and partly because LLMs err towards caution when you start talking about cybersecurity. That's the right direction to be wrong in, but it does mean you'll see things flagged as more serious than they are, and it's something we're working on. Remediation guidance is where the agents excel. After a long week on a pentest it's tempting for a human to write generic advice, and you catch yourself and try to do better. Unfortunately, you're usually limited by time and usually by not having the source code. The agents don't have either problem, so they'll tell you the line of code to change, and what to change it to on every issue. They also write about mitigating controls that can help reduce the impact of the issue, or provide a temporary fix. We're seeing that speed up how quickly people actually fix things. We had a customer with 78 issues who fixed all of them within a few days, which as a human pentester I have never seen happen. I couldn't have written the level of detail that made those fixes possible in the time I'd have had. So is AI pentesting as good as a human? AI pentesting and human pentesting are different, and once you stop trying to rank them the comparison gets a lot more useful. The agents are finding serious issues in applications that human testers have already been through multiple times. They'll read a whole codebase, work through every path in it, and write up every instance of what they find with the fix down to the line of code. And you can run one whenever you want. For what a single human engagement costs you can run four AI pentests, which means you can do deep testing on a regular basis rather than once a year. That’s a key thing that is missed by human pentesting, and often applications have undergone a lot of untested changes in between pentests. See what Intruder’s AI pentester finds in your application. Learn more. Author Written by Daniel Thatcher, Security Research Engineer, Intruder Daniel is a security researcher at Intruder with a background in penetration testing, and a focus on exploiting web applications in black-box scenarios. Sponsored and written by Intruder.

154ihqi.text: A cyber-espionage group with suspected ties to Kazakhstan has targeted government agencies across Central Asia and other former Soviet states, seeking information on diplomatic affairs, economic policy and strategic resources, according to new research. The hackers, tracked as UAT-6275 by Cisco Talos and TAG-193 by Recorded Future's Insikt Group, have conducted at least eight campaigns since January 2025, the two teams said in jointly issued reports. The Record is an editorially independent unit of Recorded Future. The campaign targeted or showed interest in government institutions across nine countries, including Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, the researchers said. Researchers said the hackers appeared particularly interested in government agencies responsible for foreign affairs, economic development, agriculture and environmental management, as well as information about regional energy supplies and water resources. “These organizations hold information that can inform negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions,” the Insikt Group said. “Across Central Asia, shared river systems and interconnected energy and transport infrastructure give such information particular strategic value.” Local clues Researchers assessed with medium confidence that the hacking group has ties to Kazakhstan. The clues include Russian-language material found in the malware, evidence suggesting that malicious software was tested from Kazakhstan shortly after it was created, and hacking activity that generally matched working hours in the country's time zone. The group's operations also overlap with earlier cyber-espionage campaigns linked to YoroTrooper, a suspected Kazakhstan-based threat actor that emerged in 2022 and has primarily targeted governments in Central Asia and neighboring countries. In one of its latest attacks, TAG-193 hackers targeted a Tajik government entity shortly after treaty discussions with Kazakhstan in March 2026. Another operation targeted a Belarusian government entity ahead of a bilateral meeting in April. Researchers said the timing could indicate an interest in diplomatic developments, although it does not establish what information the hackers were seeking or whether they obtained it. The group also showed interest in environmental and natural resource management, including an Armenian government agency responsible for environmental affairs and Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative. Hacking techniques The group typically attempts to compromise its targets through phishing emails containing malicious attachments, sometimes sent from legitimate government email accounts that have already been compromised. The emails use official-looking documents, including diplomatic correspondence, aviation forms and business proposals. Researchers said the hackers also used GitHub, the software development platform, to store malicious scripts and files, helping their operations blend in with legitimate online activity. In April 2026, the group was observed exploiting a security vulnerability in the file compression program WinRAR in an operation likely targeting Armenia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-8088, allowed the attackers to place malware in a Windows folder that automatically runs programs when a user signs in. Researchers said it was the first time they had observed the group exploiting a software vulnerability to deliver malware, suggesting it was expanding its methods beyond deceptive emails and documents. Researchers expect the group to continue targeting diplomatic institutions and government agencies responsible for managing strategic resources across the region. “Its sustained operations and adoption of additional delivery techniques suggest continued investment in gaining access to institutions holding information of strategic interest,” they added. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

rxlfj4.text: Microsoft announced that Windows Server 2022 has reached the end of mainstream support and will remain in extended support until October 2031. Microsoft unveiled Windows Server 2022 in March 2021 and made it generally available in September 2021 as a Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release with 10 years of support. "As of October 13, 2026, Windows Server 2022 has reached end of mainstream support and transitioned to extended support. The October 2026 security update is the last mainstream support update available for this version," it said. "Extended support includes security updates at no additional cost, and Windows Server 2022 will continue to receive monthly security updates through October 14, 2031." Microsoft has also extended Windows Server 2022 hotpatching until October 2027, one year after the mainstream end date of October 2026, for systems running the Datacenter: Azure Edition. Before Windows Server 2022 reaches the end of support, Microsoft advised IT admins to upgrade to Windows Server 2025, which began rolling out to Windows Insiders in January 2024 and reached general availability in November 2024. "Windows Server 2025 is the latest Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) release for Windows Server. To help keep your environment protected and supported, plan your upgrade path to Windows Server 2025 for full mainstream support," the company added. According to Microsoft's lifecycle platform, Windows Server 2025 will reach its end of mainstream support in November 2029, with an additional five years of extended support until November 14, 2034. Those who want to test it before deployment can use the free 180-day Windows Server 2025 trial available via the Microsoft Evaluation Center. You can find more information about Windows servicing dates on the Windows Lifecycle FAQ page or using the Lifecycle Policy search tool. On Tuesday, Microsoft also announced that devices running Windows 11 24H2 Home and Pro editions no longer receive security and non-security preview updates and advised customers to upgrade to Windows 11 26H2 (the latest Windows 11 version, also known as the Windows 11 2026 Update). Last week, it also warned users to upgrade devices running unsupported versions of Windows because they will stop receiving security updates after next year's Windows Update certificate rotation. 1khmvo8.text: NGINX released versions 1.30.6 and 1.31.7 on October 14 to fix five vulnerabilities, one of them present in every release since May 2005. There are three memory bugs that F5, the company behind NGINX, says could crash a worker process or possibly let an attacker run code, and each requires a specific configuration to exploit. A fourth lets an attacker forge a TLS session that could get past client-certificate checks, though F5 calls the forgery non-deterministic and beyond the attacker's control. The fifth lets an HTTP/3 client slip extra bytes into a request that NGINX passes on to a backend. None of the five was in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 15, and neither NGINX nor F5 reports attacks. NGINX rates all five medium. F5 scores the three memory bugs 9.2, Critical, on CVSS v4.0, the TLS flaw 8.3, and the HTTP/3 flaw 6.9. Which Configurations Are Exposed Every one of the five needs a directive you added: an alias with a rewrite, a regex map, AIO with SSI, a shared TLS session cache, or HTTP/3. NGINX's own documentation recommends the shared session cache and request buffering; the other condition for the HTTP/3 flaw is on by default. The TLS flaw sits in the automatic rotation of session ticket keys. Session tickets let a client resume a TLS session without a full handshake, and since version 1.23.2, from October 2022, a shared session cache makes NGINX generate and rotate the ticket keys itself unless you load keys from a file. Each worker process keeps a copy of three key slots. Rotation copied only two, so the third slot held whatever was in memory before, and a ticket naming that slot could be verified and decrypted with that uninitialized key material, "allowing a forged session," the fix commit says. F5 says the forgery works "in a non-deterministic manner that is beyond the attacker's control," and that an attacker could use it to bypass verification of client certificates. The exposed setting, ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m, is the one NGINX's documentation uses in its example configuration. NGINX fixed a session-reuse flaw with the same consequence, CVE-2025-23419, in February 2025. The conditions and workarounds below are NGINX's and F5's. The version ranges are from NGINX's advisories page. Flaw What it allows Configuration that exposes you Affected versions If you cannot upgrade (F5) CVE-2026-15176 Heap overflow in a worker process: crash, possibly code execution A location with alias, a rewrite that changes the URI, and anything that reads $request_filename (return, set, if, add_header or the access-log format) 0.1.29 to 1.31.6 Do not use alias in that location. Do not use $request_filename. CVE-2026-93479 Heap overflow in a worker process: crash, possibly code execution A regex map whose captures are referenced by root or log_format before the map's output variable 1.30.0 to 1.30.5 and 1.31.2 to 1.31.6 Use named captures, and use them only inside the block with the regex match. CVE-2026-97205 Use-after-free in a worker process: crash, memory corruption, possibly code execution aio enabled and an SSI page with include virtual commands, in some configurations 0.8.11 to 1.31.6 Turn aio off, or do not serve SSI pages. CVE-2026-95101 Extra bytes injected into a proxied request, or a body past client_max_body_size HTTP/3 with proxy_request_buffering on , the default 1.25.0 to 1.31.6 Set proxy_request_buffering off. CVE-2026-97629 A forged TLS session that could bypass client-certificate verification (non-deterministic and beyond the attacker's control, F5 says) ssl_session_cache shared:... without ssl_session_ticket_key , which turns on automatic key rotation 1.23.2 to 1.31.6 Remove the shared cache directive, or load keys from a file with ssl_session_ticket_key. Servers with ssl_session_tickets off are not affected. One Flaw Traces to July's Fix The map flaw, CVE-2026-93479, is in the string-handling code that NGINX patched on July 15 for CVE-2026-42533, a heap overflow F5 scored 9.2 that is reached through a regex map's captures. The new overflow became possible after a change in that July release, according to the fix commit. A July patch added protection against overrunning a buffer, but data could still spill into a reserved area, and a second July patch then sized the final string from that spilled length, so the string could outgrow its buffer. The commit puts limits on it. The overflow is at most the size of the reserved area on the document-root path, and a single null byte on the access-log path. F5's advisory and NGINX's advisories page list 1.30.0 and 1.31.2 as the earliest affected versions, which come before the July change. A server patched in July is inside the affected range either way. F5's July workaround had already been questioned. Researcher Stan Shaw told The Hacker News in July that switching to named captures left a narrower path open, and that upgrading was "the only complete fix." The fix commits for the alias, AIO and HTTP/3 flaws describe the other three bugs. The alias flaw opens in the moment after a rewrite changes a request's URI and before NGINX picks the next location. If anything reads $request_filename in that window, and the location's prefix is longer than the rewritten URI, mapping the URI to a file path overflows a buffer. The AIO flaw is a counter. Each pending asynchronous operation on a request adds one to an 8-bit field with no check, so 256 pending operations wrap it to zero and the request can be freed while those operations still point at its memory. NGINX names SSI pages with include virtual commands, which can run their included requests in parallel, as the trigger. The HTTP/3 flaw came from one parser field doing two jobs: holding the remaining length of an unknown frame being skipped, and the number of DATA bytes to pass on as request body. When an unknown frame was split across two reads, the leftover count was treated as body and sent to the backend, outside the client_max_body_size check. What to Do Upgrade to 1.30.6 on the stable branch or 1.31.7 on mainline. The stable release contains only fixes. NGINX publishes fixes for those two branches only, so older branches such as 1.28 stay inside the affected ranges, and a distribution package is fixed only if your distribution has backported the patches. NGINX Plus customers, and users of F5's Ingress Controller, Gateway Fabric, Instance Manager and WAF products, should check F5's advisories, which list affected builds and, for several products, no fixed build as of October 15. If you cannot upgrade yet, the table above has F5's workaround for each flaw. To see which paths your server has enabled, print the running configuration with nginx -T and search it for alias beside a rewrite, a regex map used by root or log_format, aio together with ssi, listen lines with quic, and ssl_session_cache shared without ssl_session_ticket_key. The rewrite-module overflow NGINX patched in May, CVE-2026-42945, was being exploited within days of disclosure, VulnCheck found. This is NGINX's eighth security release of 2026. F5 credits Matt Suiche of Tolmo and Mateusz Gierblinski with the map flaw, Hansol Lee of GOTROOT with the HTTP/3 flaw, PhiNode Labs with the TLS flaw, and a researcher it names as Cyberlanc3r with the AIO flaw. F5 found the alias flaw itself. NGINX also released njs 1.0.2 the same day, fixing two medium-severity XML-handling flaws in its JavaScript module, CVE-2026-101025 and CVE-2026-101019.

1n8mf91.text: Next.js released an out-of-band security update on October 14 that fixes two critical flaws allowing unauthenticated remote code execution, along with a high-severity denial-of-service flaw. One code-execution flaw is in React Server Components, and the other in librsvg, the open-source library Next.js uses through the sharp package to handle SVG images. The fixes are in Next.js 16.4.1 and 15.5.28, the current Active and Maintenance long-term support (LTS) releases. What Was Fixed The update covers three separate issues. Vercel, which develops Next.js, rated both code-execution flaws critical, each with a CVSS score of 9.5. The table lists the versions each issue affects and the version that fixes it. Issue Affected versions Fixed in Who is exposed Code execution through use cache ( GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr ) 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 16.4.1 App Router apps with Cache Components enabled, where a use cache function returns more than one typed array Code execution through SVG images (CVE-2026-96889, GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw ) 10.0.0 through 15.5.27, and 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 16.4.1, or 15.5.28 with sharp 0.35.5 or later Apps that pass attacker-supplied SVG files to sharp on glibc-based Linux Denial of service through Server Actions ( GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r ) 13.0.0 through 15.5.27, and 16.0.0 through 16.4.0 15.5.28, 16.4.1 App Router apps with at least one Server Action Who Is Affected The first code-execution flaw is in React Server Components, the React feature that runs user-interface components on the server. React's advisory covers three packages, react-server-dom-webpack, react-server-dom-parcel, and react-server-dom-turbopack, in versions 19.0.0 through 19.3.0. It describes the flaw as affecting "extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value." In a Next.js app, the trigger is a use cache function that returns more than one typed array, so only version 16 apps that enable Cache Components, the feature behind use cache, are exposed. Vercel says to upgrade even if your app has no such function. The second flaw is a memory bug in librsvg, the library that renders SVG images, which Next.js reaches through the bundled sharp package. Code execution is possible when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux, according to the advisory. By default, Next.js does not optimize SVG files. Serving them through the image optimizer requires turning on a setting called dangerouslyAllowSVG. The same library also renders images for next/og, the feature that builds social-preview images, when that feature runs on the Node.js runtime. The third flaw is a denial-of-service issue. In App Router apps that define at least one Server Action, crafted requests can push one server process to full CPU use and stop it from handling other requests. Apps on the Pages Router, or with no Server Actions, are not affected. Exposure can differ by host. Netlify said its platform does not run the image-optimizer code path and that the flaws have limited impact on its setup, while still recommending the upgrade. What to Do Upgrade to Next.js 16.4.1 if you run version 16, or 15.5.28 if you run version 15, then rebuild and redeploy. Vercel's advisory says upgrading Next.js makes package managers supply the fixed sharp automatically. On version 16 that holds, because 16.4.1 requires sharp 0.35.5. On version 15 it may not. 15.5.28 still accepts the older, affected sharp 0.34.x, and upgrading over an existing install can leave that version in place. Check with npm ls sharp and update sharp to 0.35.5 or later if it is older. If you cannot upgrade Next.js right away, the image flaw has an interim option: make sure sharp is 0.35.5 or later, or block SVG rendering in sharp with sharp.block({ operation: ["VipsForeignLoadSvg"] }), as the sharp advisory describes. The use cache and Server Actions flaws have no workaround, and only the upgrade closes them. As of October 15, the use cache and Server Actions advisories had no CVE and did not appear in the npm advisory feed that npm audit uses, so dependency scanners may not warn you about them. The image flaw does surface, through sharp's own advisory. Why the Image Flaw Keeps Returning This is the third time since August that image processing in Next.js has produced a code-execution flaw. In August, a bug in libheif, reached through sharp, allowed code execution when the optimizer handled a crafted AVIF image. In September, a flaw in next/og let attacker-controlled text change the SVG it generated. Next.js did not change its own image code this time. 16.4.1 ships the same optimizer as 16.4.0 and fixes the image flaw by raising the bundled sharp to 0.35.5, which carries a patched librsvg (2.63.2). The librsvg bug, CVE-2026-96889, was made public on September 23 and fixed in sharp on September 27. Red Hat scored it 7.8 and said exploiting it needs user interaction, such as opening a malicious file. Vercel rated the Next.js exposure 9.5 and reachable over the network. The researcher who reported the librsvg bug, Rafael B. Dias, says it is the weakness behind September's next/og flaw. A working exploit for that earlier flaw, built for one specific server setup, has since been published. sharp's maintainer also warns that whether the flaw ends in code execution or only a crash can come down to the server's Node.js build, because the official Node.js binaries are not hardened against this kind of memory attack. Not the Same as React2Shell The React Server Components flaw sits in the same three packages as React2Shell, the maximum-severity flaw disclosed in December 2025 that attackers exploited at scale. This one is far narrower. React describes it as affecting "extremely rare cases where responses transport multiple typed arrays and an attacker-controlled value." As of October 15, there are no public reports that any of the three flaws fixed on October 14 has been used in attacks.

etcx2l.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 15, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Drupal core has a critical flaw in its Field UI module that could let an attacker run code on the site's server, and fixes were shipped on October 14 in Drupal 11.4.10, 11.3.19, and 10.6.19. An attacker cannot reach the flaw through core alone, the Drupal Security Team said in its advisory. Several exploit paths exist through contributed modules, and at least one known path needs no login. Tracked as CVE-2026-108097, the flaw sits in Field UI, the core module behind the admin pages where site builders manage fields and how they display. Drupal rates it 19 out of 25 on its own risk scale, the level the project calls critical. The advisory does not name the contributed modules that open a path to the flaw, and custom code may also expose it. Drew Webber of the Security Team and Octavio Galland are credited with reporting it. What to Do Now The fixed release for each supported branch: Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.10 Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.19 Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.19 Drupal 12.0.0 beta: 12.0.0-beta2, which is not for production use No fix: Drupal 11.2.x and below, 10.5.x and below, and Drupal 8 and 9, all of which are end-of-life Both 11.3.x and 10.6.x lose security coverage in December 2026. In the week starting October 4, 151,442 of the 531,499 sites that reported their Drupal core version to drupal.org (28.5%) were on a branch that the advisory lists as affected and that received no fix. A site that cannot update yet can uninstall the Field UI module, field_ui, which "will provide protection while sites are updated," the advisory says. The admin pages for managing fields and their display are unavailable while the module is uninstalled. Field UI is installed by Drupal's Standard install profile, so a site built from that profile has the module unless someone removed it. Drupal Steward, a web application firewall service with rules written by the Security Team, already blocks some known attack vectors for this flaw. Acquia, Pantheon, Ironstar, and Skpr run it for their customers. It does not cover every possible exploit, and those sites should still update, the advisory says. The advisory rated the flaw as having no publicly available exploit code at the time of publication. As of October 15, none had surfaced, and neither the advisory nor public reports described attacks using it. The Security Team had pre-announced the release on October 12 and told sites to reserve time for it "because exploits might be developed within hours or days." In May, Drupal reported exploit attempts within two days of its advisory for a core SQL injection flaw that affected only sites on PostgreSQL, and CISA added that flaw to its catalog of exploited vulnerabilities. What the Fix Changed Field UI builds its admin tables from render arrays, the PHP arrays Drupal turns into HTML. Before the fix, the table element's pre-render step ran whatever PHP callable each table row carried in its #region_callback property, through call_user_func_array, with no check on what that callable was. Drupal's renderer has refused to run untrusted render callbacks since version 8.8 in 2019, a restriction added after earlier advisories showed that the render system could too easily call arbitrary callbacks. The renderer trusts the table element's own methods, so it ran the pre-render step, and the check never reached the callable that step then executed. The 11.4.10 code no longer calls the callback. It reads each row's region from the row's own region value and uses the table's hidden region, or its first region, when that value is not a known region. The same call had been in the code since at least Drupal 8.9.0 in 2020. In core itself, the callback is set only by Field UI's own display forms. Custom code that set #region_callback on a field_ui_table row will find it no longer runs after the update. Pantheon tells sites to check such code and to test the manage fields and manage display pages after updating. Separately, the Entity List module received its own critical remote code execution advisory, CVE-2026-108099, with the same conditions, including a known path that needs no login. Its 3.0.10 release note says the fix mirrors the Field UI change, and updating core does not update the module. In the week starting October 4, 90 sites reported using it. The same core releases also fix two moderately critical cross-site scripting flaws, in the Link module (CVE-2026-108515) and the Navigation module (CVE-2026-108514), both of which need at least a logged-in user. Drupal 7 reached end of life on drupal.org in January 2025, but Pantheon says its Drupal 7 long-term support with Tag1 Consulting has shipped Drupal 7.107 with a backport of the fix.

adtat7.text: Law enforcement authorities from 17 countries in Latin America and Europe have arrested 95 suspects in an INTERPOL-coordinated operation targeting the distribution of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) through online messaging groups. The joint action, dubbed International Effort Confluencia, included four law enforcement operations between March 2026 and September 2026. "Effective cross-border cooperation between law enforcement and the private sector has never been more urgent," said Stephen Fry, Executive Director of INTERPOL Investigation Support. "Behind every file is a child who was abused, and who is revictimized every time that image recirculates. Wherever offenders move, we have to move faster." The investigators executed 127 search warrants to arrest nearly 95 suspects and rescued a five-year-old victim whose parent had been producing and selling abuse material online. Ecuadorian authorities found one individual part of a group sharing CSAM who had approximately 15GB of abuse images and more than 4,000 files, while investigators in Panama arrested the administrator of a group disseminating abusive material depicting children with more than 700 users. In Argentina, another suspect who was allegedly in contact with over 260 girls worldwide allegedly threatened victims who tried to refuse his requests for increasingly explicit content and is now accused of sextortion of minors. Suspect arrested in Argentina (INTERPOL) ​"These platforms are increasingly used to groom children, coordinate abuse, connect offenders and receive payment for illegal content. They also enable the recirculation of abuse content, resulting in continued revictimization of children," INTERPOL said, referring to the messaging platforms used to disseminate and commercialize abuse content. "Material seized during the investigation is expected to lead to further identifications of offenders and children at risk, as well as additional safeguarding action." Last year, in February, 25 other suspects linked to a large criminal ring distributing AI-generated CSAM were arrested as part of Operation Cumberland. German cybercrime prosecutors also took down Kidflix in April 2025, one of the largest child sexual abuse material (CSAM) platforms on the dark web, and made an additional 79 arrests after identifying 1,393 suspects. European and Latin American authorities from over a dozen countries arrested 20 more suspects in June 2025 as part of a separate joint operation targeting the production and distribution of CSAM via instant messaging groups. More recently, in March, a global law enforcement action supported by Europol and named "Operation Alice" shut down more than 373,000 dark web sites that offered fake CSAM packages following an investigation that started in mid-2021. 1aw2yeb.text: Attackers are impersonating popular AI products to distribute malware, steal browser sessions, and compromise business accounts. ANY.RUN linked 1,258 public sandbox analyses to fake AI campaigns between April and October of 2026. The campaigns also increase operational pressure on MSSPs serving US businesses, which accounted for 16% of country-attributed targets. Similar attacks appearing across different customers can trigger repetitive investigations, consume analyst capacity, and extend response times, making it harder to maintain consistent service levels as threat activity grows. How Fake AI Attacks Are Reaching US Businesses Fake AI attacks pose a serious risk to business security The campaigns investigated by ANY.RUN use familiar AI brands to encourage employees to execute malicious commands, install compromised applications, or submit credentials through fraudulent authentication pages. Attackers impersonate Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, and other AI services. Their lures appear in sponsored search results, legitimate hosting services, shared AI conversations, and counterfeit download websites. Fake Copilot installation page One campaign impersonating Claude demonstrates how easily a routine software installation can become an infection. In the attack analyzed through ANY.RUN's Interactive Sandbox, the victim encounters a page resembling the official Claude download website. Clicking the Windows download button copies a command to the clipboard and displays instructions for executing it through PowerShell. Instead of installing the expected application, the command launches mshta.exe, retrieves a malicious HTA file, and triggers an encoded PowerShell execution chain. Completed analyses exposed infostealer activity ANY.RUN’s Sandbox revealed the entire infection chain The technique presents a difficult detection scenario. The employee initiates the process voluntarily, the attack relies on legitimate Windows utilities, and the malicious payload appears only after several execution stages. For MSSPs managing multiple customer environments, this creates a recurring operational challenge: the initial indicators vary, while the underlying attacker behavior remains similar. Cut 21 minutes from mean time to respond and improve SOC efficiency across your customer base. Discover how ANY.RUN strengthens MSSP detection and response workflows. Why Fake AI Campaigns Put Pressure on MSSP Operations ANY.RUN data shows that 16% of Fake AI attacks were directed at the US An individual fake AI incident may appear straightforward once its full execution chain is visible. The operational difficulty increases when an MSSP must recognize similar activity across customers with different technologies, policies, and risk profiles. These campaigns create pressure on three interconnected SOC processes. Monitoring and detection coverage: Attackers constantly rotate domains, hosting services, and AI brands, making new campaign variants harder to detect with existing indicators. Triage and escalation management: Evasive attack chains require deeper investigation, increasing analyst workload, response times, and unnecessary escalations. Threat hunting and detection improvement: Findings from individual investigations need to be correlated and reused to strengthen detection across customer environments. These challenges directly affect the metrics MSSP leadership manages: MTTD, MTTR, escalation rates, investigation cost, and SLA compliance. Improving those metrics requires a coordinated approach to monitoring, investigation, and intelligence reuse. Improving Tier 1 Efficiency Through Behavioral Investigation The first opportunity is to reduce the time analysts spend establishing whether suspicious activity represents a genuine threat. Fake AI campaigns illustrate why this matters. A suspicious download page may appear harmless until the analyst clicks the installation button or follows the instructions. Static inspection can provide an incomplete picture of the resulting execution chain. ANY.RUN's Interactive Sandbox enables analysts to reproduce these interactions in an isolated environment and observe the resulting processes, network activity, and malicious behavior. For MSSP leadership, this creates an opportunity to maintain investigation quality and SLA performance as customer alert volumes increase. 1dguhyf.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Palo Alto Networks on Wednesday issued security updates for a high-severity flaw in PAN-OS software that has come under active exploitation. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0322 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of remote code execution in the management interface. "A remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the management interface of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS software enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall," Palo Alto Networks said. The issue impacts PAN-OS software on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama (virtual and M-Series). Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected by the vulnerability. Palo Alto Networks said that no special configuration is required to exploit the issue, but said the security risk can be minimized by restricting access to the management interface to only trusted internal IP addresses. "You can reduce the risk of exploitation by restricting access to a jump box that is the only system allowed to access the management interface," it said. Patches are available in the following versions - PAN-OS >= 12.2.4 PAN-OS >= 12.1.4-h12, >= 12.1.7-h8, >= 12.1.10-h2 PAN-OS >= 11.2.4-h22, >= 11.2.7-h21, >= 11.2.10-h15, >= 11.2.13-h3, >= 11.2.16 (ETA: October 15, 2026) PAN-OS >= 11.1.4-h37, >= 11.1.6-h39, >= 11.1.7-h11, >= 11.1.10-h35, >= 11.1.13-h15, >= 11.1.16-h3 PAN-OS >= 10.2.7-h38, >= 10.2.10-h41, >= 10.2.13-h26, >= 10.2.16-h11, >= 10.2.18-h12 The network security company also acknowledged it has seen "very limited exploitation" targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface, but did not elaborate on the nature of the malicious activity involved, who is behind the effort, or when it began. The following IP addresses geolocated to the U.S. are assessed to be linked to the exploit attempts - 66.42.72[.]14 208.83.239[.]114 149.248.47[.]234 It credited Suraj Siddharudh, a senior principal product security researcher at Palo Alto Networks, with discovering and reporting the vulnerability. The disclosure comes as Cisco warned that threat actors are exploiting a critical flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway (CVE-2026-76519, CVSS score: 9.8) that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. "This vulnerability is due to improper handling of email attachments when the file reputation service is enabled," it said. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending an email that contains a crafted attachment through an affected device. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system." The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has since added both CVE-2026-0322 and CVE-2026-76519 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to prioritize fixes by October 17, 2026.

1sltudp.text: AI is already part of digital forensics and incident response work, with or without a policy in place to govern it. The issue is that these tools are growing more confident in their own output faster than practitioners are developing reliable ways to verify it. Without governance models and validation standards in place, that gap compounds and rarely stays contained to a workstation: an unverified finding can end up in a forensic report, a deposition, or in court. At SANS, we created two new AI frameworks this year to help address this challenge: the Digital Forensics & AI Investigations Framework, which we mapped to the trusted standards established by the Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence (SWGDE), and the Incident Response & AI Investigations Framework, which we mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0. Both frameworks rest on the same principle: AI can accelerate investigative work, but the human examiner remains the final authority at every phase. Where Validation Cannot Be Delegated In digital forensics, validating an AI finding starts at the source file. A tool that doesn't show its reasoning has already produced an unreliable result, regardless of the confidence score attached to it. A tool that cites the specific file it parsed — for example, a claim that browser history came from Chrome's own database — gives an examiner somewhere to start. The claim is plausible at face value, but it still has to be confirmed independently before anyone treats it as fact. I think of a high-confidence AI output the way I'd think of a third grader insisting the homework is finished. Saying it's done isn't the same as it being done correctly, and no amount of confidence changes that. The only way to know is to verify it, the way a parent checks the homework instead of taking their child's word for it alone. The mistake I see often in the field is treating AI as a single source of truth. Practitioner forums are full of the same exchange: Someone scans a file, a detector reports it as AI-generated, and that becomes the finding. The claim has no named source and no reasoning behind it, and an examiner without foundational skills has no way to catch that. What the Record Has to Show Documenting what produced a finding matters as much as checking it. Plenty of examiners say they don't use AI, while machine learning has been running skin detection, facial similarity, and image categorization inside their forensic tools for years, generating the confidence scores they rely on. Naming the tool is sufficient when AI is built into a forensic product, since opposing experts can research the integration themselves. For a general-purpose model, the exact version needs to be on record. Version history matters more than practitioners expect because casework and AI capability move on different timelines. I worked a case where the tool that would have helped with the log files didn't exist at the time of collection. By the time I testified two years later, the technology had advanced well beyond what was available during the investigation, which is exactly the kind of gap opposing counsel can use against you without a clear record of what the technology could do at the time. One Policy Cannot Govern Both Disciplines Digital Forensics and Incident Response carry different risk tolerances, and a single AI policy written for one will fail the other. Incident response has more latitude by design, because responders aren't scrutinized on every single bit and byte, and the organization needs to know what happened quickly. AI genuinely helps there, in detection and in surfacing activity a human might not readily see. Forensic examiners operate under the opposite pressure, since every source file requires validation, which is why many expect AI to add work rather than remove it. Both instincts are correct for the job in front of them, which is why the two frameworks exist as separate documents instead of one shared policy. AI capability is moving faster than human oversight can keep up with. Offensively, AI is excelling; defensively, security teams remain more cautious and slow. Closing that gap during a live incident depends on how much an organization trusts its own tooling. If a team built and validated the AI making containment or triage recommendations, then a human in the loop, monitoring and intervening rather than approving every step, is workable. Requiring sign-off on every individual action during an active incident overwhelms an analyst quickly, exactly when speed matters most. The Real Variable Is the Practitioner Every phase of both frameworks returns to one constraint. AI should never take an action that can't be undone. Evidence collection illustrates why: An investigator gets one opportunity at a sound acquisition, and a flawed one forecloses analysis entirely, no matter how skilled the analyst who comes after. Hash verification can be automated safely. Deciding how to pull cloud data, approach a scene, or deploy tools to capture lateral movement across other systems cannot be, because none of those decisions can be walked back. Legal authority follows the same logic. AI flagging that a subject has a linked cloud account is useful; AI collecting that data on its own crosses a boundary an examiner cannot undo, and some forensic tools can cross it on their own if configured to. That's the real argument behind both frameworks' operational use cases and their course mappings by phase. Whether an investigation holds up depends on the practitioner running the AI. An examiner who understands the underlying discipline and uses AI on top of it becomes more valuable to their organization. An inexperienced person using AI is the landmine, and it's leadership's job to assess that risk honestly. Building a Defensible AI Practice in DFIR Frameworks like these are as dynamic as the technology they address, and they are only effective if practitioners have the most current information and the underlying skills to apply it, knowing where artifacts live before a tool tells you, understanding what a sound acquisition actually requires, and recognizing a wrong answer when a model produces one. SANS courses including FOR498: Digital Acquisition and Rapid Triage, FOR508: Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics, and FOR608: Enterprise-Class Incident Response & Threat Hunting build that foundation across the phases both frameworks cover. Join us at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026 in December to attend FOR508: Advanced Incident Response, Threat Hunting, and Digital Forensics in person, taught by Carlos Cajigas. Learn more about SANS’s DFIR training offerings here. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Heather Barnhart, SANS VP of Curriculum.

mm9moc.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Telecom Security / Privacy The Indian government has directed telecom service providers (TSPs) in the country to mandatorily display callers' registered names along with their numbers for incoming calls starting November 1, 2026, in an effort to help people identify calls from unknown numbers and tackle spam or fraudulent calls. To that end, the Department of Telecommunications has issued a circular urging service providers to implement the Calling Name Presentation (CNAP) service. "At the time when a call is incoming, the calling name presentation service presents the calling name identity of the calling user on the user terminal of the called user," according to a circular issued by the Indian Ministry of Communications dated October 13, 2026. "Calling name identity is the name of the calling user as recorded in subscriber data record of the originating telecommunication service provider and such identity is included in the calling line identification of such user." The caller ID system is mainly targeted at wireless terrestrial networks established using 4G and higher generation technologies. The circular noted that a CNAP rollout for 2G and 3G networks, as well as public switched telephone networks (PSTNs), will be taken up separately after examination. Under the new guidelines, every time a user receives a call, the first field will display the caller's number, as is the existing practice. The second field will contain the name of the calling user in the following order of preference - If the number is already saved in the callee's contacts, the corresponding name is displayed. If the number is not saved, the calling name identity as stored in the telecom operator's subscriber database will be displayed for domestic calls. The label "International Call" will be presented for calls originating from outside India. To meet this requirement, every originating TSP is required to establish and maintain a database mapping subscribers' names to their numbers. The operator on the receiving end of the call will query this database to retrieve the calling name identity and present it to the user. Telecom operators are also expected to provide a Calling Line Identification Restriction (CLIR) facility, as part of which users can choose to hide their caller identity when making calls. Furthermore, the Ministry of Communications is urging TSPs to adopt a secure-by-design approach when implementing the system and ensure the security of communications by - Enforcing that the calling name identity is not retained upon completion of the incoming call Maintaining the quality of service in accordance with applicable laws Provisioning the necessary database, network, and connectivity infrastructure to support efficient processing of calling name identity queries Users with business connections or bulk connections can opt for a "preferred name" that replaces the calling name identity. The preferred name has to be one of the following - A trade mark registered in the name of the user as per the records of the Trade Marks Registry under the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, Ministry of Commerce and Industry A trade name of the user as registered on the Goods and Services Tax portal "For new connections, the preferred name of the user shall be recorded in both the customer application form and subscriber data record and document(s) evidencing proof that the user is registered under such name shall be presented in original to the originating TSP and true copies thereof shall be attached to the customer application form by the originating TSP," according to the circular.

1wi9qge.text: Microsoft has resolved a known issue that was causing black screens, desktop loading issues, and Explorer crashes after installing Windows 11 updates released since August. As Microsoft explained when it acknowledged the issue last month, affected users experienced multiple symptoms, most commonly a black screen after sign-in, being unable to access their desktop until they manually started the desktop session, and Windows Explorer crashes in application event logs. However, this known issue mainly affects Azure Virtual Desktop (AVD) hosts using FSLogix, a software solution that speeds up user profile loading in virtual desktop environments. Microsoft has now addressed the bug in cumulative updates released as part of this month's Patch Tuesday and asked affected users to update their systems. "This issue was resolved by Windows updates released October 13, 2026 [..] and updates released after that date. We recommend you install the latest update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one," it said in a release health dashboard update. "If you install an update released October 13, 2026 [..] or later, you do not need to use a workaround for this issue." Microsoft shared a temporary workaround for those who can't install this month's Windows updates, which requires them to manually launch Windows Explorer. This can be done by opening Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), selecting Run new task, entering explorer.exe, and clicking OK. It also mitigated the issue for enterprise customers via Known Issue Rollback (KIR), which has to be applied on enterprise-managed devices by installing one of the following group policies: Windows 11, version 26H1: KB5124006 Known Issue Rollback Windows 11, version 25H2 and Windows 11, version 24H2: KB5124010 Known Issue Rollback "You will need to install and configure the Group Policy for your version of Windows to resolve this issue. You will also need to restart your device(s) to apply the group policy setting," Microsoft noted. "Note that this Group Policy will disable the change causing this issue until a resolution is released in a future Windows update. IT admins can find further details on deploying and configuring KIR group policies on Microsoft's support website. This week, Microsoft also resolved a known issue that triggered Always On VPN connection problems after installing the September 2026 security updates and confirmed that recent Windows updates may trigger Remote Desktop failures for non-admin users if the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled.
